Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
In reply to a question put to me on Friday last, I stated that
committees have power to swear witnesses without the House authorizing them. I quote from the Revised Statutes, 1906, cap. 10, sec. 25, " an Act respecting the Senate and House of Commons:"
Any committee of the Senate or of the House of Commons may administer the oath to any witness examined before said committee.
I have noticed that motions have been made in the House to confer power on committees to examine witnesses under oath, and I have already stated that I thought this unnecessary. I quote this section of the Act now in confirmation of that view.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It may be a question as to whether the statute has appli-
 .
cation only to a committee that was so authorized by the House, and that may be the reason why motions have been made in the House to confer that power.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is quite evident that committees of the House are fully authorized and empowered to administer the oath to a witness because under another clause, sec. 24, the Senate or House of Commons may at any time order a witness to be examined under oath before a committee, provided .the committee had neglected to do so.

speechtext: Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM: I notice in a despatch which has beerr given prominence in the leading newspapers, including* the Ottawa Journal of Saturday last, a statement that wagons, harness, Ross rifles, etc., have been discarded in great quantities and left behind at Salisbury Plains. Has the Government any information on that point?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think we have any such information as that. I shall be able to give my bon. friend full information later. I believe the Princess Patricia regiment did take British rifles, because it was brigaded with a British division, but so far as the Canadian Overseas force is concerned, I have no information whatever that the Ross rifle has been discarded. The long Ross rifle, I understand from the Minister of Militia, is not i j'garded as very suitable for cavalry, not because of the rifle itself, but because of the difficulty of handling a long rifle on horseback. So far as the motor transport is concerned, my recollection is that it was subjected to very severe usage during the four or five months which have elapsed since the force has been in Salisbury Plains, arid it would be desirable, I have no doubt, that new motor transports should be sent to the front as quickly as possible; but I do not know at the moment how much of the motor transport which was so used has been taken to the front and what proportion has been left behind to be usesd during training by any further expeditionary force that may go forward.
The despatch also -refers to wagons and harness having been left behind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

wagons and harness are concerned, I am not in a position to speak; but I will get the information later on.

speechtext:
With your
permission, Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Poster) regarding the memorial that has been sent to him by the Campbellton Board of Trade, a copy of which has been sent to me by the secretary of the board, regarding the steamship service between Gaspe and Campbellton. As the House is aware from our last discussion on the matter, the minister was under some difficulty in establishing that service last year, and the best that he could do was to establish a long-distance service between Montreal, Quebec and Campbellton. But this does not meet the requirements between Campbellton and Gaspe and of the Bonaventure shore, and so they are asking that the local service between Gasp6 and Campbellton be reestablished. I have no objection to the long-distance service if it can be maintained, but the signers of the memorial are in favour of re-establishing the old semi-weekly service. Would it be possible for the minister, in view of the near opening of navigation, to call for tenders for such service? Has any action been taken in the matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is as the hon. member for Bonaventure has intimated, about the beginning of last year's service the proprietor of the line, a contractor in this ease, died. His estate was not able to carry on the service. We were in the midst of the season before this was decided, and so the best that could be done $t that time was to make an arrangement for weekly service instead of semi-weekly with a line which carried as far as Montreal. ' The document referred to by my hon. friend has been received, and is now being considered by the officers of the department. In a little while I shall be able to come to a conclusion as to what is best to be done, or what is possible under the circumstances.

speechtext:
1.	What is the latest information in the hands of the Government as to the present whereabouts of the several member's of the Stefan-son Arctic Expedition who were on board the Karluk when she was crushed in the ice?
2.	What steps were taken by the Government to rescue the members of the expedition, who are reported as not having been heard from since they left the neighbourhood of the vessel?

3.	What information has the uovernment as to the present whereabouts of Mr. Stefan-son?
4.	What are the names of the men in company with Mr. Stefanson?
5.	Does the Government intend -to take any steps to find Mr. Stefanson and his party and to aid them if they need aid?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
1 and 2. After the steamer Karluk was crushed in January, 1914, the surviving members of {he expedition landed on Wran-gel Island, where they wintered. Captain Robert Bartlett made his way over the ice and across Siberia to Emmer harbour and then across Behring Strait to St. Michaels, where he advised the Canadian Government of the fate of the Karluk. Arrangements were made to attempt the relief of the expedition, and the following ships sailed for Wrangel Island during the summer of 1914, with this object in view: the Russian ice breakers Vaigach and Taimyr, United States patrol steamer Bear, whaling steamer King and Wing, and whaling steamer Corwin. The steamer King and Wing penetrated to Wrangel Island and took off the survivors. Three members that died on the island, and two parties who left the main camp shortly after the wreck of the Karluk have not been heard of. During the winter search parties had been organized to look for these men. Wrangel Island had been explored and search parties had travelled over the ice without finding any trace of the missing parties, and the opinion of the returning members is that these parties have perished.
3,	4 and 5. The second section of the Arctic expedition is at present engaged in scientific work on the Arctic shores of Canada. They have with them, three ships commanded by navigators experienced in northern waters.
4.	Mr. Stefanson left the Alaskan coast in March, 1914, for an exploring trip north over the ice, with two men, Storker Storker-son and Ole Anderson. Before leaving he gave instructions as to measures to be taken in case he did not return the same winter. The vessel was to proceed in the summer of 1914 to the coast of Banksland and lay caches, and erect beacons for the men of the Stefanson party when they reached land in the winter of 1914-15. When the latest news of the expedition, dated August, 1914, reached the department, these instructions were being carried out. The expedition being supplied ivith three vessels does not seem, from latest advice, in need of any further aid at the present time.

subtopic: PARLIAMENTARY REPRESENTATION OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. J. HUGHES (Kings, P.E.I.) moved:
subtopic: PARLIAMENTARY REPRESENTATION OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND.
speechtext:
That a humble address be presented to His Majesty praying that he may be graciously pleased to give his consent to submitting a measure to the Parliament of the United Kingdom to amend certain provisions of the British North America Act, 1867, in order that the province of Prince Edward Island will always be entitled to at least six members in the House of Commons of Canada, that being the number of members assigned to the said province when it entered confederation.
He said: During the last regular session of Parliament the question of the membership of this House, and of the other House as well, occupied a good deal of time and attention. The fact that there was a continued and steady reduction in the number of members of this House coming from the

group of provinces known as the Maritime Provinces claimed considerable attention, and the Committee on Redistribution suggested that a change be made in the British North America Act so that no province would have fewer representatives in this House than it had in the Senate. That suggestion appeared to have commended itself to the House, and some action was taken in regard to it. However, Parliament prorogued without anything definite having been done in that regard. Hence I am bringing this resolution to the notice of the House to-day. The members from the larger provinces may perhaps wonder why we from the smaller provinces, particularly from Prince Edward Island, attach so much importance to this question. My answer to that natural inquiry would be, that in all countries having representative institutions to which delegates are sent, the small communities are always very sensitive, perhaps even jealous, with regard to the number of their representatives. While the larger provinces and the strong places can take care of themselves, the smaller provinces or communities are not so satisfied that they can under all circumstances look	after	their	own interests,	and	they	have	in consequence a sensitiveness on the question of representation. I should like the members from the larger provinces to look at this question for a few moments from our viewpoint. I think I can establish that there was in the minds of those who drew up the terms of Confederation the idea that whatever the number of members a province started with that number should not be reduced, particularly in regard to the smaller provinces. A provision was put in the Constitution to safeguard that principle. I think I can prove that when Prince Edward Island finally came into the Confederation after her stipulation for six members had been conceded, the delegates from that province were firmly convinced they were to have at least six members for all time; and I believe that the members of the sub-committee of the Privy Council with whom they negotiated the terms of the Union had the same opinion. In support of my argument, I shall quote from Sir Joseph Pope's Confederation documents, which I believe is as good a record of the negotiations as is extant. As of course the members of this House know, the first conference on Confederation was held at Charlottetown, in the province of Prince Edward Island, and was called to consider the question of a Maritime union. The public men of Canada-Quebec and Ontario at that time-had a larger idea, and suggested at the Charlottetown conference that the meeting be adjourned to meet later on at Quebec, and that representatives of the lower provinces be invited to attend to consider the question of the Confederation of the Dominion. That suggestion was carried out and the second conference met at Quebec in 1864. The province of Prince Edward Island sent certain representatives, and on looking up the records I find that those delegates were, willing to discuss any question in connection with Confederation except the question of representation. The other questions were very important of course but on the question of representation the delegates from Prince Edward Island would make no concessions. They pointed out that unless they could get six representatives that, so far as they were concerned, Confederation could not be considered. The delegates from the other provinces did not see their way clear to grant this concession, and the consequence was that when Confederation was accomplished some three years later, Prince Edward Island did not come in. I have already stated that in the minds of those who were laying down the principles of Confederation there was the idea that whatever number of members a province started with, that number should not be reduced; and the conference unanimously passed a resolution to that effect, resolution No. 21, which reads as follows:
No reduction shall be made in the number of members returned by any section, unless its population shall have decreased relatively to the population of the whole Union, to the extent of live per centum.
That provision was later on embodied in the British North America Act in subsection 4 of section 51. It was put in with the object of preserving the original representation. Under certain conditions that provision would have very far-reaching consequences. For instance, if the population of any province compared with the population of the whole Dominion was reduced in the first decade by only 4 per cent, or one twenty-fifth, no reduction in representation would take place. A basis of calculation would then be established, and if in the next decade the reduction of population in the province compared with the population of the whole Dominion was only one twenty-fifth, again no reduction in representation would take place although the population had been rereduced by ejght per cent. Supposing the same thing took place in the third decade,

that the population of the province as compared with the whole Dominion was again reduced by 4 per cent; no reduction would occur in the representation, although in those three decades a reduction of 12 per cent would have taken place in the population of the province. And so on. If, in say 50 years, a reduction of 20 per cent took place in the population of any one province no reduction would take place in the representation. But that provision did not safeguard the Maritime Provinces from reduction in their representation, although in my judgment it was thought at that time a sufficient safeguard, and if it had not been deemed a sufficient safeguard, a provision would have been inserted that would have adequately safeguarded the original representation.
The discussion of the Quebec Conference went on from day to day, and an effort was made to meet the views of the delegates from Prince Edward Island. Mr. Galt, who was very anxious to meet the views of the delegates and to have Prince Edward Island included in the Confederation, proposed that the representation of the other provinces be increased.	Mr. Brown, one of the delegates from Ontario, was, of course, very strong on the principle of representation by population.	Mr. Brown had moved a resolution which gave Quebec sixty-five and all the other provinces a number in proportion but which gave Prince Edward Island only five members. Mr. Galt made this statement in reference to Mr. Brown's motion, he proposing two hundred and twenty-five members instead of two hundred:
If we divide two hundred and twenty-five, according to population. I calculated it would give Upper Canada ninety-nine, Lower Canada seventy-four, Nova Scotia twenty-one, New Brunswick seventeen, Newfoundland eight, and Prince Edward Island six. We should commence with the census of 1861, and readjust after each subsequent census. We have supposed that the population of Lower Canada, being tolerably equable in its character, would afford the best basis. But, having respect to the rapid increase of Upper Canada, we think the Lower Provinces should not be reduced if they do not increase in the same ratio. Therefore, the Lower Provinces would have the same as they have now-
I presume that is at the time of coming into Confederation-
-unless in the very improbable case of any one falling off by five per cent or more-that is a decrease relatively to the whole federation.
That, I think, carries out the point I have been trying to substantiate, namely, that in the minds of the men laviwr the founda-
]Mr. J. J. Hughes. [
tions of Confederation the idea was present that this saving clause would be sufficient to safeguard the provinces against any reduction in their representation, and that whatever representation it started off with must not be reduced in number. The suggestion of Mr. Galt, however did not carry. Mr. Brown moved that Upper Canada have eighty-two members, Lower Canada sixty-five, Nova Scotia nineteen, New Brunswick fifteen, Newfoundland seven, and Prince Edward Island five. That carried, Prince Edward Island voting nay. Mr. Brown, in speaking to that motion, said:
The practical result will be that while Lower Canada certainly will not be less and the Lower Provinces may increase in population, they cannot decrease in the number of representatives. It keeps the House within a reasonable limit.
I think I have already stated that Mr. Brown's motion carried, Prince Edward Island voting nay. Mr. Haviland, one of the delegates from Prince Edward Island who was strongly in favour of Confederation, said:
Prince Edward Island would rather be out of the confederation than consent to this motion. AVe should have no status. Only five members but of one hundred and ninety-four would give the Island no position.
If five members out of a representation of one hundred and ninety-five at that time would give the Island no status, if we are now down to three and if the representation of the other provinces is much larger, of course our position relatively becomes much worse. There were speeches by other delegates from Prince Edward Island but all. in the same direction.
Mr. Galt was, as I have already said, very anxious to meet the views of the delegates from Prince Edward Island. And he made this statement:
It would be a matter for the greatest regreu that any difficulty should arise over this matter. We request the Prince Edward Island delegates to reconsider their decision. It would be a matter of reproach to us if the smallest colony should leave us.
In accordance with this suggestion the delegates from Prince Edward Island left the conference chamber to re-
4 p.m. consider the matter and to give their answer the next day, but before leaving Mr. Whelan, one of the delegates who was also very favourably impressed with the idea of Confederation, made this statement:
I should feel it my duty to-night to vote against the resolution, but we had better reconsider the matter. Mr. Haviland and I came

here perfectly untrammeled and without any instructions from the Government of Prince Edward Island. We understand that all proceedings were to he ' de novo ' and apart from anything which had taken place at Charlottetown. I thought that Prince Edward Island had not been fairly treated as to representation in the Legislative Council, hut I gave way on that occasion. I do not think, however, I could say I was satisfied with the representation of five m the Federal House of Commons. We are in an isolated position. Our resources are large, and our people would not he content to give up their present benefits for the representation of five members. It may be said that the confederation will go on without Prince Edward Island, and that we shall eventually be forced in. Better, however, that, than that we should willingly go into the confederation with that representation. But if the Government who formed the delegation will take the responsibility on them, I may support them.
I have already stated that the delegation from Prince Edward Island withdrew from that meeting and returned next morning to give their answer to the conference. Col. Gray spoke for the others. He said:
I am instructed by my co-delegates to _say that the provision of five members is unsatisfactory. Prince Edward Island is divided longitudinally into three counties, each returning ten members.
That is for the local legislature.
But they are always opposed to a change of representation. We cannot divide the three counties into the five members.
Mr. Brown answered:
Every province must revise its own electoral divisions to suit the number of its representatives.
Mr. Pope, one of the delegates who was afterwards Minister of Marine and Fisheries in die Government here, made this statement:
I agree in all that lias been said by Colonel Gray and Mr. Coles. But the circumstances of Prince Edward Island are such that I hope the conference will agree to give us such a number as we can divide amongst our three constituencies. Nature, as well as the original settlement of the island, has made three counties, and it would give rise to much difficulty if we had to adjust five members to the three counties. I cannot ask it as a matter of right, hut one of expediency, as one without which it is impossible for us to oarry the measure in Prince Edward Island. I, therefore, ask for six members.
Mr. Haviland said:
I fully agree with Mr. Pope. It would be an insuperable difficulty to us if we had not six members.
I do not think it is necessary to read further from these documents to show that the delegation from Prince Edward Island at that time were fully convinced that
Confederation could not be carried in that province unless they got six members to start with and six in perpetuity. I draw from these statements the conclusion that in the minds of the delegates from Prince Edward Island, and in the mind of every man at the conference, the idea was established that whatever number of members the province received that number would not be decreased. Otherwise, why lay stress upon the particular number to start with? If Prince Edward Island were to have six members for a few years only I presume the delegates from the other provinces would not have considered it such an important matter and would have yielded the point. Then, if it were only to be for a few years the delegates from Prince Edward Island would not have laid such stress upon it and would not have considered it a matter which would justify them in remaining outside of Confederation. Therefore, I come to the conclusion, and no other conclusion in my judgment is feasible, that at that period the delegates from Prince Edward Island and the delegates from the other provinces were fully impressed with the idea that the original number would not be reduced.
When the delegates returned to Prince Edward Island they were sustained by the legislature, the people, and the press. The people were willing to discuss any other feature of Confederation, but on the question of representation there was no compromise, and three years later, when Confederation took place, Prince Edward Island remained out. It appeared, however, to be the wish of the Home Government and the wish of the Government of Canada that Confederation should be rounded out by the inclusion of Prince Edward Island, and from time to time negotiations were carried on looking to that end. In 1869 Lord Granville, then Secretary of State for the Colonies, wrote to the Governor General of Canada, suggesting that the Federal Government should give liberal concessions to Prince Edward Island, and what is known as the better terms of 1869 were offered; but still we could not get the six members in the House of Commons, and Prince Edward Island would not come in. Negotiations continued, and in 1873 Earl Kimberley, then Colonial Secretary, wrote to the Governor General of Canada along the same lines as the correspondence that had taken place between the Governor General and Lord Granville, and the Governor General of Canada wrote to Lieutenant Governor Robinson of Prince Edward Island, stating that if his Government would send a delegation to Ottawa, a sub-com-

mittee of the Privy Council would meet them to negotiate on terms of Confederation. Accordingly the Government of Prince Edward Island sent a delegation here, consisting of Messrs. Laird and Haythorne, and the Government of Canada appointed a subcommittee of the Privy Council consisting of Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir Charles Tup-per, Sir Leonard Tilley, Sir Hector Lange-vin, and Mr. Howe. Negotiations between these gentlemen continued for several days. The delegates knew well the feeling of the people of Prince Edward Island on the question of representation, and this was the one point which they appeared to be determined to obtain, and did obtain, although their population entitled them at that time to only five members. So important was this point considered that it was the subject of several communications between the delegates at Ottawa and the Lieutenant Governor of Prince Edward Island, while the other conditions appear to have been left to the delegates, to make the best terms they could, although of course the financial and other terms were very important. On the 26th of February, 1873, Mr. Haythorne, one of the delegates, sent this message to Lieutenant Governor Robinson:
Probably yield six representatives.
On the 6th of March, this telegram was sent by Mr. Haythorne:
Highly probable get six representatives.
The negotiations continued and apparently the delegates from Prince Edward Island had impressed their views upon the sub-committee of the Privy Council, and on the same day, the 6th of March, the Lieutenant-Governor of Prince Edward Island telegraphed to Mr. Haythorne:
We hope six representatives will be conceded.
A conclusion seemed to have been reached on that date, because later in the day Mr. Haythorne wired to Mr. Edward Palmer, his colleague in the Government of Prince Edward Island:
Six representatives conceded.
The point upon which I have laid so much stress, and the point as to which we remained out of Confederation for six years and upon which we finally entered Confederation, was the concession of six representatives in this House. I leave it to the judgment of hon. gentlemen if they think that in the circumstances this representation was to be for a few years only. On a point which the delegates from Prince ]Mr. J. J. Hughes. [
Edward Island emphasized so much and to which they attached so much importance, is it to be thought that the sub-committee of the Privy Council with which they were negotiating the terms, would have hesitated to yield the point if that representation of six members were to continue for only a few years. I do not think so, and I do not think that any fair-minded man would come to that conclusion. There is no other intelligent conclusion to be arrived at than that the delega tes from Prince Edward Island had at all events convinced themselves that they were obtaining a minimum representation which would be permanent. The men who sat around that council board must have known what was in the minds of the Prince Edward Island delegates, and it would be an injustice to the memory and character of these men to say that they deceived the delegates, or even that they allowed these delegates to deceive themselves on that point. I, therefore, am justified in coming to the conclusion that it was in the minds of all these men who were carrying on the negotiations that Prince Edward Island was getting a concession which was to be hers in perpetuity. Unfortunately, the terms of the union were not worded so that that provision was put beyond doubt, or otherwise we would not be here to-dav looking for our rights. I can understand how easy it is for a mistake to occur even in important documents. It is known to us all that important measures have passed this Parliament, statutes drawn by the most expert lawyers, and that defects have afterwards been discovered in them which rendered remedial legislation necessary. Only a few days ago the Minister of Marine gave an illustration of how mistakes may occur in connection with the purchase of the submarines on the Pacific coast. A telegram from Sir Richard McBride stated that the price of these submarines was to be $1,150,000, but the Order- in-Council was passed for $1,050,000, and that'was a mistake which one would think could be easily seen.
The Minister of Marine and Fisheries told us that he did not know how the mistake occurred. It might have occurred in transmitting a message by telephone from the Prime Minister's office to the office of Naval Affairs; it might have occurred-probably it did occur-in the course of the work of the officer in the Naval Affairs Department who prepared the memorandum for Council. It escaped the notice of that officer, of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, of the

Deputy Minister of Naval Affairs, of the Privy Council-and was only discovered a number of days afterwards. So we see how easy it is for mistakes to occur; and in all human probability a mistake occurred in the terms of union, which mistake escaped the notice of the delegates from Prince Edward Island, of the Legislature of Prince Edward Island, and of the Government of Canada.
During the last regular session of this Parliament, as I have stated, a resolution was passed in this House to the effect that no province should have fewer members in this House than it had in the Senate. That was an effort to correct this error. Some hon. member of the House-I have forgotten who it was-told the Prime Minister that he was departing from the principle of representation by population. The Prime Minister's answer was that the departure was not very serious. And 1 say the same now. If this House should agree to give the original representation to Prince Edward Island, the departure from the principle of representation by population would not be very serious. I do not think it would endanger the Constitution. On the other hand, it would be a settlement of the question; it would lead the people of Prince Edward Island to believe that they had been fairly and generously used in this matter, a matter that to them at least is important. And any other settlement will not lead to that conclusion. We may obtain four members. That, of course, would be better than to be reduced to three or to two; but will not, so far as we are concerned, be regarded as a full or generous settlement of this question. And I say that the Parliament of Canada is big enough and broad-minded enough, and I think the men of the other provinces are broad-minded enough, to give to the smallest province of the Dominion this concession, which cannot possibly injure anybody, and which is regarded by the people of Prince Edward Island as being of great importance.
Years ago, I think it was in 1892, when the question of redistribution was under consideration, and British Columbia was obtaining a larger representation in this House than she would have been entitled to on the basis of population, Sir John Thompson spoke very strongly in favour of British Columbia's views. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, then leader of the Opposition, spoke in the same way, and said-I am not quoting his words, but I think I give with precision the effect of what he said-he would be sorry that any province of the Dominion should have fewer representatives in Parlia-21
ment than that province thought itself entitled to. That is all I am asking for. And if the right hon. leader of the Government and the right hon. leader <jf the Opposition think these views correct, if they would regret that any province in the Dominion should have a smaller representation in this House than it has always thought it was entitled to, there would be no difficulty about the passing of this resolution.
I think this matter should be dealt with this session. We may, or may not, have an election before another session, and we may, or may not, be reduced to three members. And some time or other this question must be taken up; and it would be just as well, in my judgment, to take it up and dispose of it now.
As I have already said, we of Prince Edward Island feel proud that Charlottetown, the capital of our province, saw the first conference to take into consideration the idea of Confederation. We think that since Confederation we have contributed our share towards the prosperity of this Dominion. Large numbers from the province of Prince Edward Island, as from the other Maritime Provinces, have gone into the Northwest. As a rule, I believe, they have done well there. They have cooperated with the people of the other provinces towards the progress of the West. And it is hard for us that this very contribution we are making towards the advancement of the country should become the very means of reducing our representation in this House and weakening our voice at the council board.
This, you may tell us is a matter of sentiment. To a certain extent, so it is. But it is a not ignoble sentiment. It is the sentiment that prevailed in our province before we entered Confederation. It is a sentiment, I think, that this House would be justified in considering; yes, a sentiment that this House would be justified in meeting and satisfying for all time. I place this matter before ihon. members with full confidence that they will do what they believe to be just and generous, that they will dispose of the matter in the way pointed out by my right hon. leader (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) in 1892, when he said that he would regret that any province should have a smaller representation in this House than it always thought it was entitled to.
Mr.D.D.McKENZIE (North Cape Breton): The case for Prince Edward Island has been put before the House so clearly and ably by the' hon. member for Kings, P.E.l. (Mr. REVISED EDITION

Hughes), that it will not be necessary for me to review the same history at any length. It would appear to me, from the case the hon. gentleman has made out, that it was the intention of the representatives of Prince Edward Island at the time that province entered Confederation, that it was to have six members. The question is possibly not so difficult to the mind of the hon. gentleman as it might be to myself. He is a layman, and, taking the layman's view, the difficulty would perhaps not be so striking as it is, or ought to be to me who have had, to some extent, ihe training of a lawyer. I know that the right hon. leader of the Government, and possibly the leader of the"Opposition, will say: What is the use of talking this way?-the adjustment of the terms of Confederation in relation to the representation of ihe provinces is a settled question. There was a time when this question was regarded as an open one, but a judicial interpretation of the Act was made. The matter was argued before the Supreme Court of Canada by the ablest legal minds in this country. It was carried from the Supreme Court of Canada to the Privy Council, and there received the last and, I suppose, the best, interpretation that can be given to it. That interpretation is, in effect, that the way in which the Act has been interpreted and carried out in Canada is the right way; that the representation of the maritime provinces must be reduced as the population decreases; that the reduction which we.have suffered is the proper and legitimate outcome of the Act of Confederation in which we concurred in 1867. But I wish to present to the legal mind of the right hon. leader of the Government the fact that because an Act of Parliament is interpreted by the courts in such a way as not to carry out its original intention, it does not follow that Parliament must sit back and do nothing at all. In hundreds of cases where courts have given certain interpretations of provincial or Dominion Acts, Parliament has come hack and legislated in such a way as to carry out the original intention of the legislation, regardless of what the interpretation of the courts may have been. Let me bring to the attention of the Prime Minister a particular case in point: that of the Manitoba School question. In that case the Lords of the Privy Council said that there was no doubt as to what the intention of the Manitoba Act was, but that the language used by those who drafted the Act was not of such a 
character as to ensure that the intention of the legislation would be carried out. The Government of the day thereupon introduced in this House what was known as the Remedial Bill, the object of which was not to accept the decision of the Privy Council, but to legislate in such a way as to carry out the real intention of the Act. I submit that a proper interpretation of the intention of the British North America Act as. drafted and enacted in 1867 is that the representation of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island should not be reduced. I submit that if Canada had continued to consist of the four provinces- live with Prince Edward Island-that originally entered Confederation, and if the representation of these provinces had been adjusted under the terms of the Act according to each decennial census, we should not have lost any representation in the maritime provinces.
Let me call the attention of the Prime Minister to certain conditions in the province of Nova Scotia which, I think, will appeal to him just as strongly as the representations of my hon. friend who has just moved this resolution should appeal to the Prince Edward Islanders. At the time of Confederation every county in the province of Nova Scotia was to have a member, and the county of Halifax was to have two. We had then in the province the same number of counties as we have now, all bearing the same names. If the county of Shelburne, for instance, which was one of the first counties to suffer from this interpretation of the Act, had been told at the time of Confederation that after some years they would have no representation at all; that possibly they would be joined to some other county and secure their interest in a representative in that way; would they for a moment have supported the proposal to enter into Confederation? If the counties of Queens, Cape Breton, Victoria, Pietou, Annapolis, Yarmouth, Digby, the representation of all of which has since suffered by reason of this interpretation of the Act by the Lords of the Privy Council, had been told that only for a few years would they have their original representation in the House and that after that it would be a matter of doubt whether they would have any representation at all, would the strong-minded and intelligent people of those counties have supported the proposal- to enter into Confederation? I submit that they would not.
I submit that the understanding from the beginning was that there should be no reduction of the representation originally

granted in 1867. It will be readily understood that we expected to grow; we expected that Nova Scotia and the other Maritime Provinces would keep pace with the growth and development of Quebec and Ontario, the only provinces with which they had to keep pace. The idea was that we should grow and that we should Subsequently have not a smaller, but a larger representation.
Under section 8 of the Act under which British Columbia entered Confederation, it was provided that British Columbia should be entitled to be represented by three senators in the Senate and by six members in the House of Commons, the representation to be increased under the provisions of the British North America Act of 1867. The idea of the people of British Columbia when they entered Confederation was that their representation should increase, if the conditions were such as to come under the terms of the Act, but that in any case it should not decrease. The idea of what terms of Confederation should be applied to the different provinces was then fresh in the minds of the great men who took part in framing the constitution, and I believe that they did not intend to give British Columbia any better terms than those granted to the other provinces. If the terms under which British Columbia entered Confederation were fair and right and proper, there is no reason why similar conditions should not be extended to the other provinces.
As I said a little while ago, the interpretation of sections 3 and 5 of the British North America Act stands as texture so far as the courts are concerned, but it is open to this Parliament to amend or readjust these sections. What was in the minds of the Fathers of Confederation when they drafted section 2 of the Act is, I think, clear:
It shall be lawful for the Queen, by and with the advice of Her Majesty's Most Honourable Privy Council, to declare by proclamation that on and after a Day therein appointed, not being more than six months after the passing of this Act, the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick shall form and be One Dominion under the name of Canada; and on and after that Day those Three Provinces shall form and he One Dominion under that Name accordingly.
Section 5 of the Act says:
Canada shall be divided into four provinces, named-Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
Were I at liberty to do so, I would dispute the decision of the Lords of the Privy Council on this point. It is too clear for argument that Canada must mean, and 214
meant at that time, those provinces-Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick-and that in every adjustment of representation, and on all -other occasions when it was necessary for the Legislature to bear in mind what Canada meant, it simply meant those four provinces. But the Lords of the Privy Council have held against -that view, and there is no use arguing that phase of it now. Our duty now is to press forward and legislate in such a. way as to give the smaller provinces the rights they were supposed to have obtained under the provisions of this Act.
With further reference to what was argued by the hon. member for Kings, P.E.I., I think the terms of the Act of Union of Prince Edward Island itself could very well be cited. One section reads:
That, in accordance with the terms of the said address relating to the electoral district and laws and regulations under which the first election of members to serve in the House of Commons of Canada for such electoral district shall be held, it is hereby further ordered and declared.
That Prince county shall constitute one district to be designated Prince county district and return two members.
That Queens county shall constitute one district to be designated Queens county district and return two members.
That Kings county shall constitute one district to be designated Kings county and return two members.
That seems to be straight and emphatic legislation, leaving no loophole or provision for repealing. That was what was meant to be the condition upon which Prince Edward Island came into Confederation, and I submit that it is in itself a strong argument in support of the contention taken by the hon. member for Kings that there should be some remedy by which.the operation of the Act as now understood should not result in the reduction of the representation of Prince Edward Island below the six members given to it at Confederation.
Although it is not in the resolution, and although my purpose in rising was to support the resolution of my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island, I would say that while the trouble which they have in the Island is perhaps not quite as acute in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, the whole question of the representation of the maritime provinces should be settled. We had at one time twenty-one members from Nova Scotia. After the next general election we may have only sixteen, and it is only a question of time until we shall be wiped out altogether. We still have eighteen members; after the next election we shall have

only sixteen; and while we have a Nova Scotia Premier guiding the ship of State would be a fair time to put a stop to this downhill run and restore to us the representation we had when we entered Confederation. I have much pleasure in seconding the motion made by my. hon. friend.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. A. McLEAN (Queens, Prince Edward Island):
subtopic: PARLIAMENTARY REPRESENTATION OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND.
speechtext:
I do not suppose that
any of the facts connected with the Confederation conferences are so well known to the people of Prince Edward Island, and particularly to the members of this House as the speeches delivered at the two conferences at Charlottetown and Quebec referred to by the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Hughes). Our object in this contention, wnich has been made for many years, is to impress upon this House and upon the people of Canada the fact that when we negotiated to come into Confederation, part of the contract was that we. should, for all time to come, have a representation in this House of six members. The speech which the hon. member for Kings read goes to show that that contention was made. That is a historical fact. But I contend that the contract, evidence of which is to be found on the minutes of the proceedings of this House and of the proceedings of the local House in Prince Edward Island, proves conclusively that a representation of six members was conceded to Prince Edward Island by the telegram which was sent to Mr. Hay-thorne, the leader of the Government of Prince Edward Island, by Mr. Palmer, on the 8th of March, 1872.
I have been in this House on several occasions when this question has come up. In 1907, and I think in 1908, last session, and I think the year before, this matter of the representation was brought before the House. We have never yet had a division on the question. When the Liberal partv were in power, I do not think that the r;ght hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), who was then leader of the Government, was very sympathetic with us in our contention that the contract we made in 1373 entitled us to a representation ot six members. At any rate, he did not concede us anything. No member of the Liberal party would back us up in that contention, although we claimed in Prince Edward Island that it was clear that we were entitled to six members and that the records of the negotiations showed that. Last ssesion we brought the matter before the committee which was authorized to look into the redistribution of the seats in

Canada. We had the privilege of being heard before that committee. The leader and one of the members of the Provincial Government came here and argued that there was no doubt, under the contract of 1873, that we were entitled to a representation of six members in this House. Members from the province also spoke on the same lines. When the resolution was brought down, the right hon. leader of the Government (Sir Robert Borden) did not concede that we were entitled to a representation of six members, but he inserted a clause which provided:
That notwithstanding anything in this Act, a province shall always be entitled to a number of members in the House of Commons not less than the number of Senators representing such province.
When this resolution came up in this House, I must say that, although the members to whom I spoke were very sympathetic, there was no member who rose in his seat to back the representations of Mr. Nicholson and myself, the only Island members present, in our contention that we were entitled to six members.
On the 11th June, 1914, I moved the following amendment to the resolution:
(b) Prince Edward Island shall be entitled to be represented in the House of Commons by six members. The representation to be increased under the provisions of the British North America Act, 1867. Prince county shall constitute one district to be designated 'Prince county district' and return two members; Queens county shall constitute one district and be designated 'Queens county district' and return two members; and Kings county shall constitute one district, to be designated 'Kings county district' and return two members.
I stated at the time that, while I appreciated the right hon. gentleman's concession of four members, as contained in the resolution which I have just read, and which referred not only to our province but to other provinces similarly situated. I thought that under the original bargain we were entitled to six members. The Government deserved credit, I said, for conceding us even four members, because previous governments would not recognize our right at all whenever the matter had been brought up.
So far as the representation is concerned, as proposed in the Government's resolution of last year, I realize that the Government was doing something, that we were entitled to more than was conceded to us in the British North America Act resolutions passed by the Government of this country and accepted by the British Government. I was very grateful for the small concession the resolution granted. But when the resolution went up to the Senate it was

turned 'down. The hon. member for Kings (Mr. J. J. Hughes) was not in Ottawa at that time, although he must have known that this very important matter was coming up. He went home to Prince Edward Island and neglected the opportunity, which he should have taken advantage of, for he had many friends in the Senate, and perhaps he might have been able to persuade those gentlemen to see the matter as he sees it to-day and as we saw it then. But, instead of doing that, he went to his home, and left the matter to the other Liberal members of this House. The Senate returned the resolution with this amendment:
That this Act shall not take effect until the termination of the now existing Canadian Parliament.
What did that mean? It meant that at the next general election Prince Edward Island would have only three members: one for Kings County, one for Queens County, and one for Prince County. Why did these gentlemen in the upper house do this; what reason was there for it? I can see no reason why they should have turned down the resolution. Some of the members in their speeches made distinctions between the East and the West. Some said that the right of Prince Edward Island should be recognized, that, under * the terms of Confederation, she was entitled to the representation these resolutions conceded. But, when it came to a vote, they turned the whole thing down by their amendment. The right hon. leader of the Government announced that this House could not accept the amendment made by the Senate. The hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) has spoken very well indeed on this question, and mentioned the province of Nova Scotia. Although I was present in 1914 when this matter was before the House, I do not think he had much sympathy for Prince Edward Island on that occasion. How is it these gentlemen come here now with trumpets blowing and ask for six members, when in 1914, when we had a chance to get some increase, although not what we asked for, these very same men were dumb?
I do not know what the intention of the Government is with regard to this matter, but I would respectfully ask that the Government take it into their consideration; and if they find that the Senate will not pass the whole resolution as submitted to them last session, the Government might eliminate from the resolutions that part which is obnoxious to the members of the Upper House. Personally I do not know any reason why the whole resolution should not be passed. But if that is impossible,
I repeat that it is of very great importance to the people of Prince Edward Island that their representation in this House should not be reduced; and that although they consider themselves entitled to more than this resolution concedes they are willing to accept this concession for the present and leave the matter open for future negotiation by this or some other Government. I would ask the right hon. leader of the Government to take the matter into consideration, and to introduce this session a resolution similar to the one introduced last session, providing that no province shall be represented in this House by a less number of members than that to which it is entitled to be represented in the Senate.

speechtext:
While I recognize that any discussion of the question of representation in the maritime provinces, so far as relates to [DOT] the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, must he in the nature of a post mortem, I am glad there is still life in the carcass so far as the province of Prince Edward Island is concerned. I have on more than one occasion expressed my views on this question of representation of the maritime provinces, and I can only register my regret that I was not more successful in impressing upon the powers that be the validity of the arguments and the views which I advanced to this House.
I rise more particularly for the purpose of correcting a statement which the hon. member for Queens (Mr. A. A. McLean) has quite inadvertently I believe put before the House with respect to the attitude of another chamber of this Parliament on the question of representation of the province of Prince Edward Island. It is well remembered by hon. members of this House that in the early hours of the morning when the Redistribution Bill was going through its final stage at the last regular session of Parliament, the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) rose in his place and proposed an amendment to the Redistribution Bill which provided that in the province of Prince Edward Island the number of representatives should in no case be diminished below the number of senators for that province. That amendment was accepted by both sides of this House, and it was understood at the time that it would be annexed to the Redistribution Bill to be considered by the other body of this Parliament with that Bill. For reasons which are not patent to myself at all events, the resolution of the hon. member for Pictou was not attached to the Redistribution Bill, but to another resolution having reference to an incretase in

the number of senators to be appointed from the western provinces. That resolution was held up by the Senate, or at all events so .amended that it would not take effect until after the next general election. It is most unfortunate for the contention of my hon. .friend from Prince Edward Island that the resolution proposed by the hon. member for Picto'u was not attached to the Redistribution Bill, where it properly belonged. If it had been so attached, the Redistribution Bill having passed, the amendment of the hon. member for Pietou would have passed with it and at this moment it would be the law that under no circumstances should the representation of the province of Prince Edward Island be diminished beyond the number of senators. However, that course was not adopted, and while I am not here to criticise or defend the other body in this legislature in regard to their action on the resolution respecting the increase in the number of senators in the West, I am bound to say that in my judgment the amendment of the hon. member for Pietou (Mr. Macdonald) had no place.

speechtext:
The subject which my hon. friend from Kings, P.E.I. (Mr. Hughes) has brought to the attention of the House is one which has been debated on many occasions in the House, and all that has "been put forward to-day, I think, has been brought to the attention of the House on the occasions to which I have alluded. Last year I took the responsibility of leaving the number of members for the province of Prince Edward Island blank in the Bill which was introduced, and I did that for the purpose of giving to those representing Prince Edward Island an opportunity of making their case fully before the committee and probably at greater length and with greater cogency than it might be made in a debate in this Parliament. The reasons why I thought that a desirable course to pursue were set forth in the observations which I made to the House at that time. The Bill was accordingly referred to the committee in that way. It was not, however, referred without some objection from my right hon. friend who leads the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), who said, as reported at page 847 of Hansard .
My right hon. friend, in this Bill, has refrained from making one provision, the absence of which seems to me a weakness in the Bill and I cannot but think, also a weakness on his part. He refused to determine whether or not the Island of Prince Edward is to lose a member. He left that blank and referred it to the committee for determination. I have to represent to my right hon. friend that that is a matter upon which the committee cannot have any jurisdiction; it is a matter on which this House has no jurisdiction. Parliament in this matter is not a free agent; the whole question is simply a question of arithmetic.
Then my right hon. friend went on to adduce reasons why in his opinion it was not only a weak but an improper course to take. He said, for example, this:
But when my right hon. friend leaves it to the committee to' determine whether or not Prince Edward Island shall lose one member, what will he say to my hon. friend from Pictou or any other hon. member from Nova Scotia should he suggest that it be left to the committee to determine whether or not Nova Scotia shall lose two members?
Then he illustrated in the same way in regard to New Brunswick and Ontario. Finally he said:
Therefore I regret that my right hon. friend has introduced in his Bill a principle-no, 1 cannot call it a principle, but rather a vicious feature-which might land him in very serious
difficulties were its necessary implications followed to their logical conclusion.
However, the Bill went to the committee, and the committee gave a very careful hearing, as I understand, to members of this House representing Prince Edward Island, and also to members of the Provincial Government of Prince Edward Island, all of whom put their case before the committee with the greatest cogency at their command, and the committee eventually made a report to this House. In that report the committee recommended that an address should be passed asking that the British North America Act should be so amended that no province in Canada should have a smaller representation in the House of Commons than in the Senate. If the British North America Act were so amended the amendment would take no present effect in any province excepting Prince Edward Island, the representation of which in the House of Commons it would increase from three to four members. As my hon. friend has observed, there was some discussion on the Address which I subsequently moved in this House for the purpose of carrying out that proposal and certain other proposals which are not germane to my hon. friend's motion at the moment. When that address was moved my hon. friend from Queens (Mr. McLean), who has just addressed the House, was not satisfied with it, and he moved, as reported at page 5809 of "Hansard," a resolution of entirely the same effect as that which my hon. friend has now proposed. He moved in amendment:
Prince Edward Island shall be entitled to be represented in the House of Commons by six members, the representation to be increased under the provisions of the British North America Act, 1867.
Prince county shall constitute one district to be designated Prince county district, and return two members.
Queens county shall constitute one district to be designated Queens county district, and return two members.
Kings county, shall constitute one district to be designated Kings county district, and return two members.
The hon. member for Queens (Mr. McLean) then used these words:
While I appreciate the concession of four representatives for Prince Edward Island, as provided in the last clause of the resolution. I submit that the original terms should be recognized and carried into effect. The Government deserves great credit for this concession, which is of very great importance, but I do not think it too much for me to ask that the original representation of six members should be restored.
The amendment was lost on division and the resolution as originally proposed by me

passed the House. The proposal which was reported to the House by the committee was accepted by the House, as I felt that it would not be possible for us to disregard the carefully considered report of that committee composed of five members from this side and four from the other side of the House, who had devoted a great deal of attention to the subject.
While I appreciate the spirit in which my hon. friend (Mr. J. J. Hughes) has brought this subject to the attention of the House, and while I appreciate the arguments he has put forward, I would remind him that he has argued sometimes the other way. In 1903 he took strong grounds against a motion which was proposed by Mr. Hackett, then a member of the House. My hon. friend at that time was of the opinion-I think I have his words under my hand- that it was not a question of a mistake at the time Prince Edward Island entered Confederation, but that the particular form of expression that was used at the time was the result of oversight or neglect. I do not desire to misquote my hon. friend, and therefore I give his exact words:-
I regret as much as any man can regret that the delegates at the time the province of Prince Edward Island joined the Union overlooked this important point, and did not provide against the contingency that has since arisen.
My hon. friend did not put it upon the ground of a mistake at that time; he put it on the ground of oversight, and he also took very strongly the ground (as will be found by reference to page 10909 of "Hansard" of 1903) that the long acquiescence on the part of Prince Edward Island would make it difficult to provide any remedy. Twelve years have, of course, elapsed since my hon. friend made that remark. The hon. gentleman also explained in that speech that the reason why the original representation was not reduced in 1882 was not because of reasons which had been advanced in this House, and which at one time impressed me, but was due to the fact that the census of 1881 was the first Dominion census taken after the Island had entered Confederation, and consequently that, so far as Prince Edward Island was concerned, there was no previous census with which to compare it. Therefore he argued that inasmuch as. there was no previous census with which to compare the population of Prince Edward Island in 1881, the Government of the dav found itself unable to determine whether or not the saving clause, to which he has alluded,

could take effect, and so he said there was little to be deduced in favour of the claim of Prince Edward Island from the fact that its representation was not reduced in 1882.
Under all these circumstances, it does not seem to me that the House would be justified at the present time in coming to a perfectly opposite conclusion to that at which the House arrived less than a year ago, when the motion of my hon. friend from Queens (Mr. McLean) was put to the House, which was then considering in committee, the resolution which I had the honour to propose. Further, I believe that we should be guided, as has always been the practice in this House, by the report of the committee to whom was confided the particular duty of hearing the claims of Prince Edward Island, and of hearing everything that could be said in favour of the motion which my hon. friend from Queens (Mr. McLean) proposed a year ago, and which my hon. friend from Kings (Mr. Hughes) is proposing. That report should command the support of the House unless very grave and cogent reasons can he adduced for leading the House to an opposite conclusion.
The resolution proposed by me last year went to the Senate by the unanimous consent of the House, and the Senate sent it back with a certain amendment, which by the unanimous consent of this House we refused to accept. My hon. friend from Queens has proposed that one or other of the courses he suggested should be adopted this session, and I will give to his proposal in that regard my best consideration and inform him and the House later of the conclusion at which we have arrived.

subtopic: PARLIAMENTARY REPRESENTATION OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND.
speechtext:
The members of the House know that we heard of this question for the first time, I think, in 1883, after the census of 1881, by which Prince Edward Island, for the first time, lost some of its representation irf this House. There is no doubt that the grievance as put forward to-day by my hon. friend from Kings (Mr. Hughes), and re-echoed by my hon. friend from Queens (Mr. McLean) was just as much felt at that time as it is now. But no one thought then that it would be possible to interfere with the terms of the Constitution, which provided that the regulation of representation should follow the movement of population; the representation of a province increasing or decreasing according to the result of the census.
Ten years later, in 1902, not simply Prince Edward Island but all three maritime prov-

inces, had to submit to a further reduction of representation. The grievance then became more acute, and we have heard of it from time to time ever since. All governments and all parties have had to deal with that question. All have dealt with it in the same way, concluding that, without an amendment of the Constitution, it would not be possible to grant the prayer of the people of Prince Edward Island. Last year, when the right hon. leader of the Government introduced the Redistribution Bill, he left in blank the representation of Prince Edward Island. I pointed out at the time that he had just said that it was a useless step, because this Parliament had no power in the matter, and the authority that could deal with it was the British Parliament. If there was any doubt on the subject at that time, we all agree that at present there is no doubt at all: this Parliament has no jurisdiction over^fche matter, and, even if it had, it could not grant the remedy sought by my hon. friends from Prince Edward Island, on both sides, btit would have to seek legislation to that effect from the Imperial Parliament.
Last year it was determined to seek that legislation, and it was done in a way that commends itself to my judgment, and I think commends itself to the judgment of hon. members generally. The committee to which was submitted the question of redistribution came back with a report that this House had no power to give to Prince Edward Island the representation it wanted; on the contrary, the committee had agreed to reduce the representation of Prince Edward Island from four to three, because they could not do anything else. A member of the committee, the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), made a suggestion. There was at that moment a petition pending before this House to increase the representation of the western provinces in the Senate. The hon. member for Pictou suggested that if this petition were granted by the two Houses of this Parliament, and if, in consequence, the Imperial Parliament were to be asked to pass the necessary legislation, advantage might be taken of the occasion to have an amendment of the Constitution made, providing, not for granting all that was asked for by Prince Edward Island, but that the prayer should be granted to this extent, that the representation of any province in the House of Commons should not be less than its representation in the Senate.

speechtext:
At dissolution. I have not the amendment of the Senate before me, but I am quite positive that it provided that this section should come into force not after the general election, but at dissolution. When Parliament dissolved, therefore, the Act would come into force, and the province of Prince Edward Island would be entitled to four members. The amendment was not accepted, however, and the Act remains on the Statute book without it.
It is not worth while arguing as to what was done or what was not done by the Senate; I have only to say this to the hon. member for Queens (Mr. McLean) and to the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Hughes).
I am well aware that the province of Prince Edward Island has felt for many years that it has been unfairly dealt with, because its representation has decreased with each succeeding census. But if the representation of the province of Prince Edward 
Island has been moving down, that decrease has been in accordance with the Act of Confederation; the province has obtained the representation to which it is entitled under the terms of that Act. My hon. friend says that Prince Edward Island would not have come into Confederation unless it had been assured of at least-six members. When it entered Confederation, Prince Edward Island, according to its population, was entitled to only five members. The province did not want to come into Confederation unless it had a representation of six members, and the men of that day, very properly I think, nit being inclined to quarrel upon such a trifling point, granted them six. No provision was made at that time that the permanent representation of the province should be six members. This want of foresight applied not only to Prince Edward Island, but to Nova Scotia arid New Brunswick as well; no one of the fathers of Confederation-neither Sir John Macdonald, Sir Charles Tupper, nor anybody else-anticipated the great development which has taken place in the West, and which has reduced the population of the eastern provinces. This grievance is not peculiar to Prince Edward Island; it applies to Nova Scotia and New Brunswick as well. With census after census the three maritime provinces have seen their populations decrease. But representation by population is a fair and just principle. If the population of a province increases, the province is entitled to additional representation, whereas if its population decreases, its representation decreases also. So absolutely fair is this principle that the men responsible for government, either on the one side or the other, have hesitated to deviate or depart from it. It was proposed last year, by the committee that reported upon the Bill then under consideration, that the matter should be settled in this way: henceforth no province shall have less representation in the House of Commons than it has in the Senate. That was a departure from the principle, but it was, after all, what seemed to me to be a fair compromise. The larger western provinces-Quebec, Ontario and the young giants in the West-are too strong to have reason to begrudge the slight increase in representation which this would give to the eastern provinces. We accepted that compromise-for my part I was glad to support the committee in that respect- and it seems to me that our friends in the maritime provinces ought to be satisfied that in so doing we endeavoured to dispose

of this irritating question in a fair and just manner.

speechtext:
I was very careful, Mr. Speaker, in the few remarks which I made upon this subject, to avoid saying anything at all that would have a party colour, because I think this is a question which can be and ought to he settled without resorting to party politics. I regret, however, that the senior member for Queens, Prince Edward Island (Mr. McLean), did not feel disposed to pursue a similar course. I regret to a still greater extent that the right hon. Prime Minister did not pursue a similar course. If I understood the hon. member for Queen's correctly, in speaking on this subject a few moments ago, he made a statement that is not borne out by the facts. He sought to leave the impression that on account of the action of the Senate, the Government was prevented from passing legislation which would give the province of Prince Edward Island four members at the next election. That matter has been pretty well cleared up since the hon. member sat down, and I am sure that he now feels that he made a mistake. He must realize that no action taken by the Senate when this matter was before them, operates to prevent this Government from passing an Act or from completing legislation, which would come into force upon the dissolution of this Parliament, to give the province of Prince Edward Island four members at the next election. My hon. friend, therefore, was mistaken in that respect, as he generally is.
The hon. gentleman went out of his way a little, I think, to mention the fact that I was absent from the House when this matter was finally considered during the closing days of the regular session of 1914. It is true that I was absent, just for a few days. I was informed by a member of the Redistribution Committee a few days before Parliament closed that the chairman of the committee had told him that the question of redistribution would not come up for consideration at that session therefore I left for home a few days before Parliament prorogued. The Redistribution Committee or the Government changed its mind, however; Hhe matter was brought up, anu I could not possibly find time to get back. But I wish to say to the senior member for Queens that if he were as attentive to his duties as I have been, whether on the Government side or in Opposition, he would not be in the position that he is in to-day. He would be certain of nomination when he goes back to his constituents, and would not have to
importune the Government to give him a position to save him from his friends. The hon. member knows that he will not be nominated.

speechtext:
We shall know in a few months. The truth of this matter will be all explained to the hon. gentleman's constituents in a few months from the present time.
Now, with regard to the right hon. the Prime Minister, I regret that a man of the ability of the right hon. gentleman should think it necessary to go somewhat out of his way to represent to the people of Prince Edward Island that I was not thoroughly orthodox on the question of representation. The right hon. gentleman brought up this matter in 1914 and referred to a speech which I made in 1903, in answer to Mr. Hackett, then a member of this House. This speech did not happen to be indexed, and the right hon. gentleman must have waded through "Hansard" for eleven years to find some statement of mine that he could twist or construe into an (argument against the representation of Prince Edward Island, while at the same time pretending to be a friend of Prince Edward Island on this subject. I had spoken two or three times as strongly and as favourably as I could for the views of Prince Edward Island on this matter, and these speeches had been indexed; but the right hon. gentleman did not quote from any of these, all the time pretending to be a friend of Prince Edward Island and wading through "Hansard" year after year to find some statement made by me that could be twisted into an argument against Prince' Edward Island on this point.
The right hon. gentleman went farther than that. He said I had made the statement that it was too late to raise the question. The right hon. gentleman is a

shrewd enough man to know that my statement was that it was too late in the day for Mr. Hackett to raise that question in order to make political capital of it. I think perhaps I had -better read my remarks. This is the conclusion:
Therefore I think it is altogether too late for my honourable friend and his political associates from Prince Edward Island to try to make political capital out of it at this time.
I referred to the fact that when the first reduction took place the Conservatives were in power and the hon. gentleman then speaking had raised no objection. That was an innocent remark to make, and I do not think it would bear the interpretation the right	hon.	gentleman put	upon it.
The	right hon. gentleman said in
effect that he might have got over that unfortunate speech of mine if I had not used the word " overlooked " or " oversight," but he said that was a terrible word to use and was equivalent to negligence or incompetence. I find in the International Dictionary the definition of the word is " an error committed through inadvertence." That was just what I meant, an error committed by the delegates through inadvertence, and I am sure if my right hon. friend wished to do something for Prince Edward Island that word would not have prevented him. I am soTry if anything I said prevented the right hon. gentlemen from doing what he would wish to do for Prince Edward Island. He said that the delegates wlho came here to argue this question before the Redistribution Committee and before the Government-the Premier of the. Island and Mr. Stewart-had presented clear, cogent and strong arguments. I find that they used the word " unforeseen." I do not think there is a great deal of difference in the meaning of the two words, and if in their statement, which was written, by the way, so that they would have time to choose their words, they said that unforeseen contingencies had arisen. If that was a suitable word, the word "oversight" would not be so unfortunate. The right hon. gentleman in his course in this matter, reminds me of the characters in the Old Curiosity Shop, where Codlin told Little Nell not to pay any attention to Short, that Codlin was her friend, not Short. Codlin wanted to be the friend of Prince Edward Island, not Short; if they would have nothing to do with Short and cultivate Codlin, he would see them through. My friend Codlin has the opportunity; I would be pleased if he would see the matter ]Mr. J. J. Hughes.[
through and give to Prince Edward Island that which he has always contended he would be inclined to give, provided he had an opportunity and power to do so. I hope it will not be a case of Codlin and Short.
