For a copy of all complaints to the Government of the killing of one American citizen and the shooting of another by militiamen, in the-waters of Lake Erie, and of all correspondence with regard to the same with the British Embassy and American authorities.
He said: The community some weeks ago was shocked when it heard that two American citizens in the waters of Lake Erie had been shot by three Canadian Militiamen, one being killed and the other wounded. What .1 saw in the newspapers led me to believe that these men were trespassers-that they were in our waters and were poaching and were at that moment violating the laws of Canada. The boys who shot them, three young militiamen, are now in durance. They are to be subjected to trial, and I would say nothing to prejudice them. On the contrary, I believe that they acted according to what they thought was their duty, and, for my part, I give them credit for having no wrong intentions. Perhaps they were too hasty in using the rifle, but that is the only thing with which we might reproach them.
I understand that the Government have since that time made what amends they could by agreeing to pay $10,000 to the relatives of the one who was killed and $5,000 to the one who was wounded. In this the Government have followed the right course, and I commend them. They have done what in their power lay to alleviate whatever bad feeling may have been caused. They have preserved the peace between ourselves and our neighbours, and that is an essential element in the case. For my part I would approve of anything done by the Government with a view to repairing as much as possible the injury done, even though the men who were shot were trespassing and breaking the law.
My object in making this motion is to call to the attention of my right hon. friend a very similar case, about which my right hon. friend was questioned some time ago in this House. I refer to the case of Nottar, a French reservist, who had gone to Montreal to book his passage to France, where he was going to take up arms with

the rest of his fellow-countrymen. Nottar was shot by a sentry under circumstances very similar to those to which I have just alluded. There was this difference only, that, while the victims in the Fort Erie shooting case were trespassers, Nottar was not a trespasser. He was endeavouring to discharge his duty to his mother country. He was challenged by the sentry. He did not answer as soon as he should have done, perhaps because of a difference in language, the sentry having challenged him in English and he understanding only French. He passed on, and the sentry shot him. It is to be regretted-and if the Minister of Militia were here I should have less hesitation in saying what I have to say now- that the Minister of Militia seems to have given the order that sentries were to shoot to kill. At all events, in the early days of the war our sentries were too prone to make use of their rifles. But there has been no such action since. I rise to say that the relatives of Nottar are just as much entitled to compensation as the relatives of those American citizens who lost, one his life, and the other his limb; but Nottar has an even stronger case, I think, and I commend it to my right hon. friend that his family are just as much entitled to compensation. My right hon. friend stated the other day that he had received no application from Nottar's family, but was informed that they were bringing an action against the sentry who committed the act. That is equivalent to an application to the Government; for, if the courts determine that the sentry went beyond his duty, the Government would very properly assume the condemnation and seek to indemnify Nottar's family. It is for these reasons that I have brought this matter to the attention of my right hon. friend.

After some
*question had been asked in the House about Nottar's case, I asked my colleague the Secretary of State to ascertain as precisely as he could the circumstances of the case and the position of the litigation, which I understand is pending. He informs me that the solicitor representing Nottar's family has promised to send us full information on the subject within a week. When that information arrives we shall take the case into consideration. I admit that there is a good deal to be said in favour of what my right hon. friend has put forward to-day as to the propriety of granting compensation to this man's family.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend has alluded to sentries having been somewhat too prone to shoot in the early days . of the war. We must always bear in mind that at that time we were facing very unusual conditions and that there was a great deal of excitement as to the possibliity of an attempt to destroy buildings in which munitions of war were kept, and other buildings in which preparations for war could be carried on on an extensive scale. I am not aware that my hon. friend the Minister of Militia has ever used the language that has been attributed to him in his instructions to sentries. On the contrary, I have found him disposed to have them fully cognizant of the responsibility placed upon them. But at the same time one can realize that a sentry placed in an important position and under the conditions to which I have alluded, might find himself in danger of reprimand if he did not enforce pretty strictly the instructions given to him by his superior officers.
So far as the Fort Erie shooting case is concerned, there is no objection to bringing down such papers as are not of a confidential character; nor should I have the slightest objection to my right hon. friend perusing the entire file, which is pretty voluminous. Immediately after the unfortunate incident had occurred, we took steps to ascertain the facts as far as we could. Having ascertained-tliese facts to a certain extent, through the Attorney General of the province of Ontario and by inquiry of the military authorities, we sent an expression of regret to the Government of the United States at a very early date. Afterwards, when the proceedings at the inquest were available, further communication took place over the telephone with the Attorney General of Ontario, and we ascertained his view after perusal of that evidence, whereupon, on the sixth day of January, a despatch was sent to His Majesty's Ambassador at Washington, which perhaps I might read for the information of the House:
Referring to my telegram January 4th. Shooting at Fort Erie. From information received from Attorney General of Ontario as to nature of evidence given at Coroner's inquest, it appears that object of shooting was deterrent, as deceased and his companions were unlawfully engaged in shooting out of season and that injury which resulted in death of deceased was entirely unintentional. Nevertheless Government of Canada are of opinion that person guilty of shooting ought to be placed on his trial and steps will be taken for that purpose. In view of circumstances which so unfortunately resulted in death of deceased, Government of Canada consider that as an act of grace, suitable compensation should be made to family of deceased and to person injured by shooting.

Communication was had afterwards through the ambassador at Washington, and by direct negotiation through the Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs, Sir Joseph Pope. Eventually an arrangement was arrived at by which, as my right hon. friend has stated, we agreed to pay, and have since paid, $10,000 to the family of the unfortunate man who was killed and $5,000 to the man who was wounded somewhat severely and was in hospital for some time. There was also an arrangement made by which certain expenses of solicitors and others who were engaged by the representatives of the deceased man, and by the person who was wounded, but survived, should also be defrayed by the Government.
The accident was unfortunate in many respects. It would be unfortunate, of course, that this shooting should have taken place under any circumstances. It was particularly unfortunate that the persons, one of whom was killed and the other severely wounded, should have been citizens of the . great and friendly nation to the south. We thought that under the circumstances it was our duty to express, and we did express, immediate regret, and we also thought-and I am glad to know that my right hon. friend agrees in that view-that under the circumstances, and as an act of grace, it was proper for this country to make compensation. I am glad to be able to assure the House that the course which the Government have adopted in that regard is entirely satisfactory to the Government of the United States and also satisfactory to the persons who were acting for the family of the deceased and for the unfortunate man who was wounded.
1 do not desire to lay before the House any of the circumstances which were detailed to us through the military inquiry which took place, nor do I think it a desirable thing to dwell upon the evidence which was given at the inquest. The whole circumstances will be under judicial consideration early in March, when these men will be placed on their trial, and it would neither be desirable nor proper that we should make, in advance of the trial, any observations. This, however, may be said, that the men, as I understand, were asked to go to the assistance of an officer of the province of Ontario who had observed the two men trespassing on the Canadian side, and he was of the opinion that they were violating the game laws of the province of Ontario in what they were doing. He has stated, I believe,

and it has been stated by the men also, that there was no intention to wound or kill either of the persons so engaged, but merely to deter them from. proceeding in that which they had undertaken and, if possible, perhaps to induce them to come to the Canadian side and submit to the jurisdiction of the country upon whose territory they were in fact at the time the shooting took place. I shall be glad to bring the papers down at the earliest date. If my right hon. friend should desire to peruse the confidential correspondence, I shall be glad to place it at his disposal for that purpose.

subtopic: VOTES FOR ELECTORS ON ACTIVE SERVICE.
VOTES FOR ELECTORS ON ACTIVE SERVICE.
speechtext:
It has seemed to me proper that this Parliament should at the very earliest possible moment assure our volunteers that if the war is prolonged until an election should take place, they would be permitted to vote. I am quite satisfied that the majority, if not all the members of the House, agree with the principle of my motion, although I am quite prepared to hear that some may question the practicability of carrying out such a scheme, so as to secure a proper representation of the vote of the men absent on service. I find, that the principle for which I contend has been recognized by legislation in Australia and in New Zealand. In Australia, the Commonwealth Electorate Act of 1902 provides for ordinary absentee voters registering their votes, and some of the provisions of that Act might be incorporated in a Bill to attain the object I have in view. Under the Commonwealth Electoral Act, absentee voters are entitled to vote by mail, and the procedure is briefly'this: they apply to the returning officer for a 'ballot, and certain persons, including justices of the peace and postmasters are authorized to take the ballot of the absentee, and as authorized witnesses must certify that he knows the voter who has exercised his franchise and that he has voted upon the ballot supplied to him. That has general application to absentee voters, but an Act passed last year by the Legislature of New Zealand deals specifically with the Overseas force. It is called the Expeditionary Force Voting Act, 1914, and under its provisions every member of that force who was sent from New Zealand to serve in the war for His Majesty, is entitled to vote.
I take it from this that the right to vote is not confined to those whose names appear upon the voters' lists. Under the Canadian Enlistment Act, a young man of 18 years is eligible to become a volunteer, whereas he would not be eligible to vote, and it would be a matter for consideration whether we should give all our volunteers, regardless of age, the right to vote, or whether we should confine that right to those whose names appear upon the voters' lists in Canada, and who would have voted had they been in their constituencies when an election occurred. Another provision hi the New Zealand law is worthy of attention, and that is the recognition that it would be almost impossible for an absentee voter to vote for any particular candidate, and the provision therefore is that he shall have an opportunity of voting either for the Government candidate or for the Opposition candidate,
and of course the Labour party being a very strong party in that country, he also has an opportunity to vote for a supporter of it. The voter therefore votes for his party and the vote is assigned by the Prime Minister for the Government and by the leader of the Opposition for the Opposition, and by two members of the Labour party if he votes for that party. Technically speaking, there is no government when Parliament is dissolved -and the Act has a 'special clause which says, that "Government" and "Opposition" means the government and opposition in office at the -time of the passing of the Act.

subtopic: VOTES FOR ELECTORS ON ACTIVE SERVICE.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman know how that Act worked out in practice last election?

subtopic: VOTES FOR ELECTORS ON ACTIVE SERVICE.
speechtext:
I cannot say what the result was in the last election. In view of the fact that the principle of such legislation has been recognized in Australia and New Zealand, it does seem to me that a law could be framed by this Parliament which would give effect to the object my motion has in view.
It is a question whether a ballot should be supplied, or whether the volunteer should not be allowed to write on any piece of paper his choice at an election, and that paper, safeguarded, let us say, by the commissioned officer of his company writing his name on the back and stating that this is the ballot of so-and-so of such-and-such a company and such-and-such a corps and forwarded to the returning officer. Then, provision might be made that every returning officer should notify some officer in charge of the force of the dissolution of Parliament, that officer to notify the commissioned officers of the opportunity which the volunteers would have of exercising their franchise in this way. Copies of the Act, when passed, could be distributed by the Canadian High Commissioner, for example, for those who are now at the front, and by the Militia Department sending to the volunters a copy of the Act when they proceed to the front. Certain penalties are provided in the New Zealand Act which could be provided in ours also. On the whole, it seems quite feasible for us to frame an Act which would give to our volunteers an opportunity to exercise their franchise should an occasion arise. I understand that there is at present a committee of this House dealing with the electoral law, and I think this matter might well be referred to that committee for action, * should the House be of opinion that we should make such an amendment as I propose.

subtopic: VOTES FOR ELECTORS ON ACTIVE SERVICE.
speechtext:
Has the hon.
gentleman in mind any machinery by which it would be possible to have the absent elector seized of the issues presenting themselves at a general election?

subtopic: VOTES FOR ELECTORS ON ACTIVE SERVICE.
speechtext:
I think the volunteers are
at present seized, and perhaps more strongly than we are, of certain features of what may be in issue in the campaign. They are, and must be, in almost daily communication with their parents or relatives in this country. For example, I have in my possession a very interesting letter from one of the volunteers at the front-I presume he is at the front; this is dated from Salisbury-in which he deals with the question of boots for the soldiers which is agitating the country at the present time. He expresses a clear opinion on that subject, and if the House is interested I should like very much to read the letter. It would show hon. members that our soldiers are familiar with what is going on at home. It seems to me that no difficulty would arise under the head suggested by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark). The volunteers would be seized of-one of the issues at all events, and that is, what this Government has done to take care of them.

subtopic: VOTES FOR ELECTORS ON ACTIVE SERVICE.
speechtext:
That is not a party issue.
Mr. J. H. BURNHAM (West Peterborough). As the seconder of this resolution, I would say with all due deference to the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) that there is nothing in the Election Act requiring a man, as qualification for voting, to know one thing of what is going on in the country. The hon. member's objection would be valid if the right to vote were conditional on such knowledge; but it is not. In order to vote, a man must be a British subject, not less than twenty-one years of age, a resident of the electoral division, and-

subtopic: VOTES FOR ELECTORS ON ACTIVE SERVICE.
speechtext: And go it blind.

subtopic: VOTES FOR ELECTORS ON ACTIVE SERVICE.
speechtext: Others go it blind besides the men at the front. I cannot see, on general principles, what justification there can be for withholding from the men who are defending this country at the front with their bayonets, the right to do the same with their ballots.

subtopic: VOTES FOR ELECTORS ON ACTIVE SERVICE.
speechtext:
This might be feasible if clear-cut issues were presented to the people. But we must remember that the candidates are nominated only eight days before polling, and in some counties both candidates are
[Mr. Fripn-l
on the same side of politics. It would be pretty hard, at such a distance, for the soldiers to decide between the candidates. Many candidates would not even be known to these electors. I think it would be hard to devise any machinery to enable the soldiers to cast their votes intelligently.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
subtopic: VOTES FOR ELECTORS ON ACTIVE SERVICE.
speechtext:
The resolution of my hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Fripp) is undoubtedly a very important one. It is a resolution that requires, in my humble judgment, very calm, reasonable and fair consideration at the hands of hon. members of this House. I am sure I express the earnest hope and wish of every hon. gentleman within the four walls of this Chamber, when I say that it is to be hoped that it may not be necessary to have a general election in the Dominion of Canada before the termination of this terrible war. But there is none the less great importance to be attached to the suggestion of the hon. member. We are living in a time of rapid change and have to be prepared to deal with new conditions. The hon. member for Ottawa has referred to the legislation of the Commonwealth of Australia under which a system has been devised for the exercise of the franchise on the part of their soldiers who have gone to the front in defence of their country and their flag. But I am a little afraid that the Bill of the Commonwealth of Australia would not apply in so far as the Dominion of Canada is concerned. Should necessity arise for a general election, I am sure there is no man in this House or out of it who would like to deny the right of the franchise to the good, loyal citizen who has gone to the front in defence of the flag, and to fight our battle for the greatest possession of the people of Canada, our British citizenship, and for the maintenance of our membership in the great British Empire. However, I have not had time to discuss this matter with my right hon. friend the leader of the Government, who has just taken his seat, and I have no doubt that he will suggest wnat is the best course to be adopted with regard to the subject matter of the resolution now before the House.
Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM: I am not sure that the attitude of my hon. friend the hon. Minister of Public Works in this instance will not go down as one of the famous retreats under proper cover. I, like the Minister of Public Works, hope that there will be no necessity for a general election in Canada until this war is over. In fact, 1 would go farther, perhaps, than some of my

[DOT]937
associates in clearing the way so that there
need not be any election, so far as constitutional law is concerned. I understand that the New Zealand Act has not yet been made operative; consequently we cannot tell how it would work if an election were brought on during the war. I agree with all that has been said as to the wisdom of allowing our volunteers to exercise their franchise. They are defending, in a more practical way, perhaps, than we in this Parliament are- that citizenship which gives us the right of free franchise. They are doing their utmost to protect our rights as citizens of the country whicn we think is the freest in the world, and I would not think of doing anything to deprive them of the privilege of exercising their rights if some practical scheme could be worked out under which they could do so in a proper way. For some years the introduction of a system has been advocated in Canada to enable commercial travellers to cast their ballots without being obliged to return to their constituency and lose perhaps a week or more of valuable time. Up to the present no practical result has been attained along this line, for reasons which presented themselves to those in power heretofore and which are, no doubt, apparent to those in power at the present time. If our volunteers were all in Canada, the difficulty of working out a scheme of tliis kind would not be so great, because Canadian laws and regulations would be applicable no matter in what part of Canada the volunteers were at the time of the election. But the large majority of them are in a foreign land, many thousands of miles away, and they cannot have full information with regard to the candidates or as to the various conditions which prevail, a knowledge of which is quite necessary. Besides, there is no way, so far as I can see, of enforcing a Canadian Election Act in a foreign country. Certainly the difficulties are very great. Secrecy would be another extremely difficult thing to enforce in an army, the men composing which are scattered about, some in the trenches and some in other sections of the fighting line, working under conditions which we can scarcelv comnrehend. Then, again, I can hardly imagine that the soldiers fighting shoulder to shoulder in the trenches for the rights of the British people and the continuance of the liberties which we all enjoy would have any time to differ with each other on matters which to them would seem at the moment comparatively trivial. I think it would not be prudent to do anything which might sow the seed of discord among our soldiers who are neither 22
Grits nor Tories, French nor English, Irish nor Scotch, but British citizens fighting without any division for what they believe to be right. It strikes me that their time will be fully taken up with the great work in which they are engaged. In saying that, J do not combat the principle at all, but it strikes me that a Bill should have been placed before the House so that we might have been enabled to see if there is any practical way of working the thing out. But were we to commit ourselves immediately to this principle without being sure that it is practicable, we would not be treating the question as seriously as its importance deserves. The adoption of some scheme might prove beneficial, or, again, it might cieate discord among the men-and unquestionably there should be no discord among them. I do not wish to be too emphatic in the matter, but I see almost unsurmountable difficulties in the way of our trying to apply this principle to our volunteers, particularly to those outside our own country. As to those who are in Canada, I think the modus operandi might be worked out if it were thought desirable.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: VOTES FOR ELECTORS ON ACTIVE SERVICE.
speechtext:
I was not aware that the motion of my hon. friend was coming up this evening, nor have I had an opportunity of giving much consideration to the subject, which is not without importance, that he has brought to the attention of the House. It would seem to me, in line with what my ihon. friend the member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) has said, that a great many difficulties would be encountered in working out legislation based on this proposal. To carry on an election in this country under the present statutory provisions, which are the result of a great many years' thought and frequent careful revision, is not unattended with difficulty; so that the proposal that men who are fighting for the Dominion and for the Empire should participate in an election by casting their votes thereat while abroad, is	a	subject that
certainly demands	the most careful
consideration. I am not aware of the provisions of the New Zealand Act. I have never seen it, nor do I know of the existence of such a legislative provision in New Zealand except by references which I have seen from time to time in the press. It has been stated in the press that that Act was invoked in respect of New Zealand's expeditionary force. I am not at all sure that the statement is correct, but I remem-

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
ber that it was reported that some elections depended upon the returns of the voting of the expeditionary force. It is possible that my hon. friend the hon. member for South Renfrew is correct in what he has said in that regard. It would be undesirable for us to refuse consideration to the proposal which the hon. member for Ottawa hap brought to the attention of the House; on the other hand, it would be even more undesirable that we should embark upon any such proposal without giving it very careful consideration. So I would suggest to my hon. friend from Ottawa that the best course would be to refer his proposal to the committee which has already been appointed for the purpose of taking into consideration certain amendments to the Act respecting Controverted Elections, and I therefore move that all the worus after the word " that " in the proposed motion be left out and the following substituted therefor:
The select committee composed of Messrs. Northrup, Maclean (Halifax), Murphy, Carvell, Robidoux, Bennett (Calgary) and Doherty, be authorized to inquire, consider and report to this House whether legislation should be passed at this session providing that electors of Canada who have enlisted for Imperial service or are engaged in active service be enabled to exercise their franchise at any election that may occur during their absence <>n such service, and whether any other legislative provision ought to be made with respect to the matter.
Amendment agreed to, and motion as amended agreed to.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I understand that the
hon. member is moving this resolution at the request of the hon. member in whose name it stands, but who, owing to indisposition, is unable to be present. I presume that would be satisfactory to the House. I am afraid that this resolution cannot very well be moved by a private member, because it affects postage and therefore really involves a contribution of public money.

The hon. member for
Rouville is unfortunately indisposed, and I understand that, acting under the advice of his physician, it will be a couple of weeks at least before he can again take his seat in the House. This afternoon he asked
ISir Robert Borden. 1
me, through a fellow member, if I would move the resolution in his absence. The late Postmaster General I presume, at the time was familiar with the rules of the House. The adoption of such a resolution may or may not compel the Government. Decisions have been rendered pro and con. During the time I occupied tne Chair the point was raised several times. Some Speakers have decided that such a resolution is binding on the Government, but others have decided in a contrary way. It is at the request of the hon. member for Rouville that I am moving the resolution. We have heard something about the volunteers to-day. This is not a party question, but merely a friendly move towards the boys, giving an opportunity to their friends in Canada to send letters or newspapers free of postage. It is a thing that will appeal to the House. Of course, I am prepared to leave the matter in the hands of the Prime Minister.

speechtext: If carried in the affirmative, the resolution will practically commit the House to an expenditure of money, and therefore it should be moved only by a member of the Government.
It might be considered either advisory or compulsory; I believe there are opinions both ways. Under the circumstances, could we let the motion stand for the present as if it had not been moved?

Yes.

What is the explanation of this increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The reason for the increase in this appropriation is that the department intends to pay out of it the maintenance and repairs of the following steamers, in addition to those whose expenses have been formerly charged to it: Aranmore, construction, N.S., Quebec and Hudson Bay, Halifax; Bellechasse, river St. Lawrence ship channel, inspection and staff boat, Quebec; Grenville, lighthouse and buoy service, Upper St. Lawrence and lake Ontario, Prescott, Ont.; Lambton, construction, Great Lakes, Parry Sound, Ont.; Rouville, construction, Gulf of St. Lawrence, Quebec.

These expenses were formerly charged to the boats, but we thought it more correct to bulk them into this one item. That accounts for the increase.
Have any new icebreakers been put in commission during the last six months?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
Requests have frequently been made to me that an ice-breaker be sent into Gaspe bay early in the spring. Was any action taken in that regard last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No. The difficulty is that we can not comply with all the requests we receive for the services of ice-breakers. We are worse off now than last year, because we have sold the Earl Grey to the Russian Government to keep the White Sea open during the winter. We regretted having to part with her, but, under the circumstances, felt we ought to comply with the Russian Government's request. We have an ice-breaker in course of construction by the Canadian Vickers at their shipyards at Montreal, but for reasons hon. gentlemen will understand the date of its delivery has had to be postponed considerably.

The condition of Gaspe bay has become almost famous since the departure from that place of the Canadian expeditionary force. In the inner bay there is a lot of floating ice, which takes two or three weeks and sometimes more to break up, and delays navigation accordingly. It is just the same between Dalhousie and Campbellton. The route is blocked at both extremities. If ever the minister has an opportunity of sending an ice-breaker down there, I am sure it would be appreciated.
How much was received from the Russian Government for the Earl Grey?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: One hundred thousand pounds in round figures. The exact figures were given to the House to-day in reply to a question. It was $495,000.00.

I should like a little explanation of an item I have seen in the press. Several advantages have
resulted from the work of the ice-breaker. I think it was last year I submitted a report to the House showing that it was believed that the navigation up the St. Lawrence to Montreal, in consequence of the work of the ice-breakers, was 'being advanced perhaps ten days or two weeks and in some cases more, depending on the season.

Examiners of masters and mates, ?16,500.

Is it advisable to permit teachers who have had charge of instructing men who are up for examination as masters and mates to conduct the examination of these men and pass upon their qualifications? It is regarded as convenient if it is permissible.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It has never been permissible.

I do not see why it would not be permissible. A man who has attended college, has his degree, and has become a professor or a teacher ought to be more than usually competent. He does not get anything for the work of conducting an examination of this kind and I fancy it would be a great convenience. It is hard to understand why, if he is a capable man to teach these candidates, he should not be equally capable to conduct their examinations and pass judgment upon their qualifications unless there was. some special advantage to himself in passing them. We have a school in the town where I live presided over by a very capable man and when some of the pupils attending that school wanted to go up for examination I understand that a man was sent from Halifax to examine them, whereas, if a local man could examine them, it would be less expensive and more convenient. When a man was ready to go up for 9 p.m. examination he could be examined without having to wait. As it is now, I understand that if they want to go up for examination, unless there are five or six of them ready to be examined, the examination cannot be conducted and the result is that men who are ready to pass their examination are kept back.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is raising a question about which there is considerable difference of opinion in connection with ordinary educational work. There are some people who contend with a good deal of force too, that the instructor is better qualified to conduct the examination of his pupils than any one else. There are other people who hold that the instructor should not conduct examinations, but that a fairer and more intelligent examination can be obtained by having examiners who have not been connected with the instruction of the pupil. There are some universities in this country that I know of in which degrees are awarded on examinations conducted by educationalists who are not instructors in the institutions. They feel that a teacher might have some prejudice against, or leaning towards, a certain pupil and that if they get an outsider who simply takes the pupil, having no personal knowledge of him, they may get a fairer examination in that way. The practice which has always prevailed in the department in connection with the examination of masters and mates is that examiners are appointed by the department. There is a regular examiner at Halifax, Captain Malcolm, and if any one in my hon. friend's neighbourhood wants to try the examination Captain Malcolm will be sent there to conduct it. It is not necessary to wait until there are four, five or six, or any number of students to be examined although the attempt is made to get as many together at the same time as possible. If there is only one man who is prepared to undergo examination he does not have to wait until there are several candidates, but the examiner will be sent down for that purpose. Naturally, we try to have a number of applicants together in order to save expense. This system is open to discussion. There is a good deal, I frankly admit, to be said on both sides of the question of whether the examiner should conduct the examination or whether the instructor should do it. Perhaps it is as well to have an examiner who is appointed by the department for that purpose and in whose knowledge, skill and experience the department have confidence.' Perhaps that would cause greater confidence to be reposed in the results of the examinations and certificates given by the department than might be the case under the system which my hon. friend has spoken of. This is the system which has always prevailed and I think it would hardly be wise to change it unless the arguments presented were very strong the other way.

for masters and mates, I take it that the system applies to salt water or would the minister send an examiner to any part to examine candidates for masters or mates?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My desire is that the students shall have every opportunity to pass-the examination. speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not think so.
Why should he not have a reduced rate on the Intercolonial railway?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will discuss that with the Minister of Railways.
And I doubt very much if the Minister of Railways will be willing to consent.

The civil servants get reduced rates on the Government railways.
Investigation into wrecks, $18,400.
Who is the Wreck Commissioner?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Mr. L. A. Demers, who is a very old official. Mr. Demers retired from the position at one time and became Harbour Master at Montreal and Captain Lindsay was appointed Wreck Commissioner. About a year ago Captain Lindsay was appointed to the commission in connection with the pilotage service, and Captain Demers was appointed to his old position in the department. The Wreck Commission is a court consisting of the Wreck Commissioner, who is chairman and two nautical assessors. The practice is for the Wreck Commissioner, in holding an inquiry at Quebec, St. John, Halifax,* or elsewhere, to select two seamen of experience to act with him as assessors. The authority for the assessors is signed by myself, or whoever may be minister. He makes inquiry and gets the two most experienced sea captains, old sailors, he can find, and they act with him as assessors. The finding of the court has to be signed by the Wreck Commissioner and at least one assessor. The item this year is $10,000 less than last year. That is accounted for by the fact that last year inquiry had to be made into the loss of the Empress of India. For that purpose a special court was appointed. We estimated the expenses of that court at $10,000. This year no such special court is provided for.

The signing of the warrant in blank is almost like a cheque to buy militia horses. The report of the Wreck Commissioner on the Empress of Ireland

disaster, I suppose, cannot be taken as evidence in the civil suit now pending?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not know what the
laws of evidence are in the province of Quebec-whether evidence taken before a properly constituted court be accepted in another court. By agreement it could.
How many wrecks are investigated in a year? How many were investigated last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In the fiscal year the number of wrecks investigated was thirtv-four, exclusive of the Empress of Ireland, which was invesigated by a special court.

Is there any report of
the court in the Empress of Ireland disaster?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: A very full report has been published. I suppose it would be right that that should be laid on the table. That had not occurred to me, but I see no objection to bringing it down.

It would hardly be
useful unless it is printed.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is printed. If the hon. gentleman is interested, I shall be glad to send him a copy.
I shall be thankful for it. Perhaps other members also would like to have copies, unless it is too expensive.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
If I find we have enough
copies, I will act on the hon. member's suggestion and send one to each member of the House.
The hon. gentleman said that Captain Demers, with two sea-captains-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That is the word I used,
but they need not be sea-captains in the literal sense. They ought to be marine men, but both not necessarily sailors. In certain cases one might be an engineer, for instance.

The point was as to
appointing men to examine into wrecks on the Great Lakes. I had occasion to speak to the minister last year upon this matter. The conditions on the Great Lakes are entirely different from those on the ocean. Without going into details, I may say that, so far as Captain Lindsay is concerned, he was a wreck commissioner to investigate the wrecks that occurred in the storm of the 9th November, 1913, perhaps the greatest that ever visited the Great
Lakes. Some findings were made in the case of the Arcadia by the wreck commissioner, Captain Lindsay, who is wholly a deep-sea man that, in my opinion and in the opinion of many masters-I believe, in the opinion pf ninety-nine per cent of those masters-were wholly erroneous. Had Captain Lindsay understood the Great Lakes as well as he understood deep-sea sailing, he never would have made such findings. I am not going into a dissertation on the evidence, which I have before me, nor into the findings themselves. But, from my knowledge of the Great Lakes, having lived upon them all my life and having some knowledge of marine matters, I think that in justice to the masters and mariners upon those lakes, and in justice to the department itself, no wreck commissioner should be appointed to investigate wrecks upon the Great Lakes except one who has had experience in sailing on the Great Lakes and knows absolutely the conditions of that navigation. I think the minister must agree that sailing on the Great Lakes is vastly different from deep-sea sailing. On the lakes they have	not	the room that	they	haveat	sea	and	cannot	go	abouttheir	course in the	same way. In	manyother ways also the navigation differs. I am not pretending to find fault with the department	except in the	case of the
Arcadia, in which the finding was erroneous. I throw out these suggestions in order that in future wreck investigations men may be appointed upon these occasions who are familiar with the navigation conditions of the Great Lakes.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend from West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) called my attention to this fact during last session. A delegation waited upon me composed of gentlemen interested in the navigation of the Great Lakes, introduced, I think, by my hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Middle-bro). I was very much impressed with their sincerity, and it was perfectly clear that they believed the course that 'had been pursued was not fair to the navigation of the lakes. They asked that a Wreck Commissioner should be appointed for the Great Lakes besides those for the Atlantic and Pacific. But in view of the small number of wrecks on the lakes within the last few years I thought it not wise to appoint a Wreck Commissioner; but I did give positive instructions that when there was investigation of a wreck on the Great Lakes or inland waters, the Wreck Com-

missioner should see to it that the two assessors he selected to advise him should be navigators familiar with the navigation of the lakes. I hope that will meet the case. Certainly, we have had no complaints since. The hon. member refers to the case of the Arcadia. He will remember that I told these gentlemen there is a provision in one Act for an appeal, that appeal being to the Minister. It has to be taken within a certain time. But my recollection' is I told these gentlemen that I would waive the time limit, if they wished to appeal to me and would hear the appeal. I think the power of the Minister in such a case is to order another inquiry before the same commissioner or before some other. However, the matter did not proceed further. They said it would not be convenient to get it up then, but I said I would hear it later in the season. But I believe they thought it better to leave the matter as it was. It is still open to them, however, to bring in an appeal if they desire to do so, and if they take that course I shall give my best attention to the matter.
I think the decision of the minister along the lines mentioned will be quite satisfactory.

Following this inquiry
into the disaster to the Empress of Ireland, have any changes been ordered by the department with regard to the dropping of pilots by steamers at Father Point?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, we are carrying out the recommendations made in that respect. It may be necessary for us to obtain permission to build another boat some time in the future in order to have it done thoroughly. My hon. friend will understand that I have endeavoured to cut out of my estimates this year as much capital expenditure as possible; consequently they have been very considerably reduced. We are acting entirely in accord witli the recommendations made by the commission especially constituted by this Parliament, of which Lord Mersey was chairman, and this year arrangements will be made which will obviate any danger previously arising from the source referred to.

Will the minister state
briefly what was the result of the inquiry into the stranding of the steamer Canada at Ste. Anne des Monts?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have here two lists of investigations. The first list is one of investigations into wrecks during the fiscal

years 1913 and 1914. In this list I find: " Canada, stranding; no one to blame." The other list is one of investigations into wrecks during the period from April 1, 1914, to February 4, 1915, in which I find, under the heading " Canada, stranding," the following: f' Master reprimanded, and mate suspended for three months."
Are any particulars given as to how the accident happened?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
Has the Canada been in dry-dock this year?	-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Canada is not a
government boat; I do not know whether she has been in dry-dock or not.

The Canada in wtiieh I
am interested is a boat subsidized by the Government, which is about to begin a new service. There has been a good deal of talk about this wreck, and I am anxious to know what position the matter is in at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This boat receives a subsidy from the Department of Trade and Commerce.

Before a subsidized boat
begins a season of navigation under contract with the Dominion Government, is it inspected by any officer of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: All boats are inspected by an inspector of hulls and an inspector of boilers and must obtain certificates from these inspectors before they are allowed to go on route.
Are the results of these examinations made public in any way? Are they accessible?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
They are available in the
department to any one who wishes to see them.

The Canada is a very
old boat. She used to be known as the Copatriot, and belonged to a French company navigating between Baie des Chaleurs ports and St. Pierre Miquelon. Her name was changed and she engaged in service in Chaleurs Bay. She has met with several accidents, and the people want to know whether the boat is seaworthy or not. I was told that last year and the year before she should have gone into dry-dock.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The boat cannot go on route unless a certificate is obtained from the inspectors of hulls and boilers.
The certificate of the suspended mate is in force this year, then?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, after the lapse of the three months.

Who is holding wreck investigations at Quebec; Captain Lindsay?
Mr. HAZEN; Captain Lindsay does not hold any wreck investigations. These would be held by Captain Demers.

I understand that during the summer an investigation was held as a result of which a certain person was held to blame. Subsequently another investigation was held, and the same person was exonerated because of the fact that the gentleman who conducted the first investigation was unable to understand the parties who were called to testify. Would the minister give me some particulars in regard to this matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think that was in respect of the inquiry into the case of the Montfort. Senator Choquette appeared as counsel for the officers of the ship, and after the inquiry was over he complained that neither the wreck commissioner, who at that time was Captain Lindsay, nor the assessors were able to understand the French language well enough to enable the man whose conduct was being examined to make a proper defence. As a result of this a re-hearing was granted, of which Captain Lindsay was chairman and Captain Demers was one of the assessors. In that way the difficulty was overcome.

I should like to draw the attention of the minister to a statement made to me by a person whom I believe to be entirely trustworthy, to the effect that some of the steamers which are navigating our maritime waters at the present time are unseaworthy. I would like the minister to give definite instructions to the inspector of hulls with a view to securing a proper test of the seaworthiness of these boats. In order to ensure that the boats are actually seaworthy they should be subjected to a practical test involving the placing in the boat of a weight equal to that ordinarily borne by it in the carrying of passengers and crew. I have every reason to believe that the statement made to me is correct, and I believe there should be no difficulty whatever in seeing that proper and sufficient tests in that respect are made in the future.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If the inspectors of hulls- so far as I know they are competent mencarry out their duties and the instructions given to them, no vessel will go to sea that is not in a seaworthy condition. The same applies to the inspector of boilers, whose duty it is to examine the machinery and to see that it is in proper condition before the vessel is allowed to go to sea. Before appointment these gentlemen have to pass an examination to the satisfaction of the officers of the Marine Department, and the instructions given to them are of a very explicit character. I shall, however, examine those instructions more thoroughly and see if they are sufficient.

We hear certain strange
stories from pilots, engineers, captains, etc., about the unseaworthy condition of such and such a boat. Is the minister certain that the inspections are properly and thoroughly made? I heard many stories in connection with the Canada that I do not care to repeat. Is the department in a position to know that the work of inspection is very thorough and full?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They make reports to us of their personal inspections of every single boat and these reports are in the department. Their instructions are to make most careful examinations, but in view of what has been said I think we shall send out a special circular letter to the inspectors calling their attention to the instructions received and pointing out that there is some alarm in the public mind that the inspection is not sufficiently thorough and telling them to see that the examination is as thorough as possible.

I do not expect the
hon. members who have spoken to inform the House who are the owners of these steamers that are said to be unseaworthy, but it is extremely dangerous that steamers should be plying along the coast of Nova Scotia or anywhere that are dangerous, and I think it would be well for the hon. members to convey privately to the minister the names of the steamers referred to in order that there may be a thorough investigation.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
If my hon. friends have
any particular steamers in mind, if they will come to the Marine Department we shall show them the reports on those steamers.

The only complaint I have
heard in reference to the inspectors in our part of Nova Scotia is that they are too strict. I doubt very much whether there are any owners of steamboats who would dare

to send boats to sea in an unseaworthy condition and without the certificates of the inspectors of hulls and boilers. As I understand, there is a heavy penalty for operating boats which are not regularly inspected.

There seems to be some misunderstanding as to my meaning. I did not mean that the steamers themselves were in an unseaworthy condition, but that the boats they carried had been lying on the decks for a long time and had become dry, and my informant did not think that .they would support the number of passengers they are supposed to carry in an emergency. His idea was that the inspector should put the life boats in the water when making an inspection, and put in them a weight equal to that of the number of passengers they are supposed to carry. I shall be glad to give to the minister a list of the boats that have been mentioned to me.

It is part of the duty of the inspector to inspect the life boats just as he does the life preservers, etc.
Expenses of schools of navigation, $8,000.

What is the explanation of
this item?
- Mr. HAZEN:	This item is intended to
cover the expenditure in connection with the department's free navigation schools already established and to provide any extension of the service that may be undertaken in the fiscal year 1915-16. Free navigation schools are now in operation during the whole year at Quebec, Halifax and St. John, and during the winter free navigation schools are operated at North Sydney, Collingwood, Vancouver and Carleton. The hon. member from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) brought the necessity of that part of the country to my attention last year, and we established a school at Carleton, in Bonaventure county.
Who is the instructor?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Captain Landry.
Has the result been encouraging?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: According to the report, the new school opened at Carleton, Bonaventure, on the 1st of December last, under Captain Landry has had an 'average attendance of six pupils and these will be ready for examination for certificates about the middle of February. There has been an average attendance of six pupils, and it cannot be said that the school is a failure.

For the first year that is very encouraging. Will the school be con-
tinuied at Carleton or moved along the coast to other parishes, .say Bonaventure?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Does the hon. member think there is a site 'better adapted for the school than Carleton?

Bonaventure has some
three thousand people. It is farther east than Carleton.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I .shall consider the desirability of changing the location.

Does the minister say that
there is a free school at Yarmouth?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Conducted by whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Conducted by Captain John E. Murphy.
That is news to me. I knew that Mr. Murphy delivered lectures there during the winter, but I never heard that, he was running a free navigation school.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It would perhaps be more correct to say that lectures on navigation are delivered during the winter at the places I have mentioned.

Is the course completed
in one year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not necessarily. As a rule the pupils who go to the school are young men who have had experience on the sea, and have studied more or less. Then they attend these lectures for a certain time and a good deal depends on their aptitude and cleverness as to the length of time that the course will take.
The minister will understand that my only object is to give the various districts an opportunity of benefiting by the schools to as great an extent as possible.

The school in the town of North Sydney is doing excellent work. The attendance is getting larger every year, but we should like to see it larger still.
I notice from the newspapers that the technical college at Halifax has added navigation to the subjects taught there. I understand there is some co-operation between the college at Halifax and the department at Ottawa. Perhaps the minister could give us some explanation of that arrangement, if any, and what assistance the department is giving in paying teachers.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes, we entered into an arrangement with the technical college at Halifax. They provide the accommodation,

fuel and that sort of thing, and we provide the instructors and equipment. We pay the instructor, Capt. John Simmons, $80 a month. I will just quote from Mr. Burnett's report of the school:
The Halifax school is making good progress. It was opened 1st April, 1914, and has been in operation continuously since. Captain Simmons, the instructor, has been in constant attendance every day and evening except Sundays. The attendance since the summer months has been good. For November and December the average daily attendance was seven pupils. Several of those attending the school have already passed examination and received certificates as masters or mates. Others after attending the school for a while, go to sea to return at a later date and finish the course. Others will be ready for examination in the spring. Thirty-one candidates have already passed at Halifax for certificates since April last.
Have any applications been made to the minister for a school of this kind in Charlottetown?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not know of any.
We are a sea-faring people down there, and have turned out a good many captains who have sailed all over the world.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Is there a private navigation school at Charlottetown?

Yes, but the pupils have to pay a fee. If men in other parts of the maritime provinces can get tuition free or partly free, the department is discriminating. I am sure the teacher in that college would be glad to work under the Government and relieve the pupils to that extent. It is desirable that our young men should be encouraged to qualify themselves as masters or mates, and as the Government are helping in other parts of the country, I now make application and press it as strongly as I can for similar assistance to be given to the school at Charlottetown.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In places where a well-conducted school seems to be meeting the needs of the case, the department has always been very careful not to interfere with the gentleman conducting such a school. There have been no applications from Charlottetown for assistance of that kind since I have been minister; so evidently the people there are pretty well satisfied with the present state of affairs. However, I will look into the facts of the case.

I am not suggesting that the minister establish a rival school, but I think he should take advantage of the school that already exists there. The Government might supplement the instruction,
or make it less expensive to the many young men who wish to get an education, but find the fees of a private school too high. The very fact that a private school is being successfully conducted there, would indicate that a competent instructor could be easily got.
Removal of obstructions in navigable waters, $20,000
Mr. A. AY. CHISHOLM: What comes under that?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Perhaps I can best explain by giving what we paid out in 1914-15 for removing these wrecks. The steamer Charles Crawford, Lake St. Clair, Ont., $1,450; steamer City of London, Lake Erie, Ont., $4,900; sunken moorings, Grand Manan, N.B., $75; steamer Electra, Mar-garee Harbour, N.S., $150; old hulk, Guys-borough, N.S., $70.45; schooner Annie R. Lewis, Barrington, N.S., $454.50; steamer Elfin, Charlottetown, P.E.I.. $500. Up to the present we have spent $7,599.95. This money is for removing obstructions in navigable waters. Where the owners of a sunken barge or ship cannot be got to remove it quickly enough, the department removes it in the interests of navigation and charges the cost up against the vessel owners, and collects if possible. Sometimes we succeed in collecting, and sometimes not.
Are you collecting the cost of removing the wreck at Mar-garee Harbour?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Captain LeBlanc removed
that at a cost of $150, which we are trying to collect.
How does the minister select these persons for removing obstructions?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We advertise for tenders.
How are these tenders advertised?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
By public posters in the
district.

I am afraid the minister is ill-informed in respect to that. Mv information is that instructions were sent down to the Patronage Committee and that they selected Captain LeBlaric. If the notices were sent down there, they were never posted up. Nobody knew about the work except the man who got the contract, and he got it through the Patronage Committee. I have no doubt the minister has acted in good faith, but to say that public

tenders were asked for the removal of that wreck is not correct. Notices were not posted up. That is my home, and I know all about the circumstances, what it cost to remove the wreck, who did the work, and how the choice was made. I wish to impress upon the minister that this man was selected by-the Patronage Committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I never heard of the matter before. The deputy minister tells me that the usual practice was followed. These posters are printed, sent down and posted up in different parts of the district. Tenders are asked for the removal.

These posters were
not put up; nobody knew anything about them until this man came along and removed the wreck.
Winter mail service, $11,000.
From where to where?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This is from Cape Traverse to Cape Tormentine.
The service is in operation now?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

Is that for the
small boats?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The amount spent during
the last fiscal year was $7,566. The amount spent during the present fiscal year, up to 31st December, was $2,218. Something, of course, depends upon the severity of the winter. The vote is used for the ice-boat service.
How many boats are employed?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The number of men employed is 74 and there are twelve boats altogether.
This vote is for the winter of 1916?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is for next year.

Is it not supposed that
the car ferry will be in operation then?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Then we will not have.to spend any of this vote. The car ferry would have been completed by now but for the war. When the war broke out the British Admiralty took charge of the shipyard in which the car ferry was being built and put this work to one side as other work for the navy had to be undertaken. This has caused delay. I do not know whether the ear ferry will be ready next year or not, but if it is this vote will not be wanted.

The war could not very
well have caused the delay in completing the car ferry because the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) told me during the regular session that the car ferry would be in operation by the 1st of August and the war did not break out until the 4th of August. I do not see how the war could have prevented the construction of a ship that was to have been completed, on this side of the water and in operation by the 1st of August.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There was a great deal of work done for the navy before the war broke out.

Yes, in anticipation of
the war.
The Minister of Railways will have to explain that.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
You will have to wait
until he comes.

This vote has proved
that the Government are a little doubtful as to whether the car ferry will be a success. Of course, I am glad to see that they are making provision to have the mails carried in any event. The fact that the Earl Grey has been taken away and sold to the Russian Government is unfortunate for that service. Perhaps it could not have been helped, perhaps there was a reason for it and we hope she is doing good service where she is, but if this had not been a very mild winter there would have been a very poor service between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. The Minto and Stanley were put into that service and notwithstanding the mildness of the winter they were caught in the ice and were unable to perform the service. If that condition continues and next winter should happen to be severe the people of Prince Edward Island will suffer a great deal because of the war. Their communication will be cut out and I sincerely trust that every effort will be made to try and have the car ferry in operation before next winter. We have been waiting for it for a long time, we have been promised 10 p.m. it and something always happened to prevent it being put in operation. This vote gives an indication that in the mind of the Government we will have to wait a while yet.
Inspection of live stock shipment, $5,000.
What is that for?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It is our business to see that live stock shipped through Canadian

ports is shipped in such a manner that it does not suffer during the voyage, that the stalls and places where the animals are confined are suitable for the purpose. We spent $2,400 last year. There are two inspectors at Montreal and we used to have an inspector at St. John. I did not see any reason for the continuation for the office at St. John and the work is now discharged by the agent of the department there.
Mr. MARCH,:	Has the minister the
number of cattle shipped from Montreal, Halifax and St. John?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The inspectors of live stock shipments at Montreal report that 134 horses, 512 cattle, 97 mules and 296 sheep were shipped to Great Britain from the 1st May to the 20th November, 1913. This year's report has not been received.
Mr. MARCH,: That is a great falling off from the previous years?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There has been a great falling off in the shipment of live stock from Canada of late years.
To continue subsidy for wrecking plants

Quebec. Maritime Provinces and British Colum-bie, $45,000.
What wrecking plants are there in Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The wrecking plant in Nova Scotia is provided by the Dominion Coal Company. They maintain a wrecking plant which is divided between Halifax and Sydney and which will be placed at the disposal of shipowners and others requiring this service whenever required. Steamers and tugs are located at Sydney and Louis-burg and also at Halifax.

What steamers are
located at Louisburg?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The tugs Duglas Thomas and C. M. Winch are located at Sydney in summer and Louisburg in winter. The steamers located at Louisburg in summer are the Cabot, the Cacouna, the Cape Breton and the Louisburg; of course they are not there all the time.

Is there any report
from the Dominion Coal Company on the services they rendered last year as a wrecking concern?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is such a report.

Complaints have been made that the Dominion Coal Company, as a wrecking concern, is not a success. Unfortunately, and what is a very unusual
thing, three foreign vessels went ashore in a dense fog, on the island of Scatari, last summer. The consul of the nation to which one of these ships belonged complained that they could not obtain any assistance from the Dominion Coal Company.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Do you know the names of these ships?

I do not; but one of them was a Norwegian vessel1. I do nut make any complaint, but I think it is only fair to say that these vessels are not what might be called stationed at Louisburg in the summer, nor would that be contended for by the company. These vessels are carrying coal between Sydney and Montreal in summer and it is quite possible they may be for a little while at Louisburg, but they do not load coal there unless they are going to Boston or some New England port. I bring- this matter to the attention of the minister so that he may make inquiry into what service the country is getting for the money paid to the Coai Company as a wrecking concern.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I will make inquiry. 1
understand my hon. friend to say that a complaint has reached his ear from the Norwegian consul or from some other consul. I can understand that persons may not wish to make a public complaint but if my hon. friend will send me the facts privately, I shall be much obliged to him. We want a proper service for money we pay and if we are not getting it we should know the reason why. If my hon. friend can give me privately more information than he would like to give in the House, 1 will have the matter very thoroughly inquired into, without involving names.

I shall be happy to get particulars from the person I have in mind, and I will hand the information to the minister. I can assure the minister that I hav- nothing at all but the most friendly relations personally with the Dominion Coal Company, but if they are getting money out of the treasury of this country they should certainly render a suitable service for it.
Did the minister say there is a wrecking plant at St. John?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I said that during the winter the tug Springhill of the Dominion Coal Company was located at St. John. In addition to that, this winter, in consequence of representations we received, and there being a large amount of shipping in St. John, we made arrangements with the company that supplies the wrecking plant at Quebec, and

they stationed the large tug Strathcona with pumps and wrecking appliance, at St. John for service in the Bay of Fundy. The arrangement I made with that wrecking company was that we would guarantee them five thousand dollars. If they earned five thousand dollars we would have to pay nothing, but we had to ensure that they would receive five thousand dollars in any event. I think the arrangement was a very good one. Of course, if there was a wreck of any importance, they would easily earn an amount larger than we guaranteed.
Did any of these boats come to the wreck of the Navarre, bound from St. John to the old country, which occurred near Yarmouth, about the beginning of this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I know that our own boats went down there, but I am not certain as to the Lord Strathcona. However, I have no doubt she was available if her services were wanted by the owners of the ship.

I am very sorry the minister did not carry out the recommendation which I made to him last year, and I shall now repeat it. A great many wrecks occur at the mouth of the Bay of Fundy south of Yarmouth.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not so very many.

Quite a number; almost every winter there are one or two steamers wrecked on the Gaunet Rock ledges or some of the Tusket islands. Last year I recommended that the minister should enter into an arrangement with Messrs. Hugh Cann and Son, Limited, of Yarmouth, who have a large number of boats, to look after wrecks that occur in that vicinity. If the minister had taken my advice, he would have a more satisfactory arrangement than that which exists at present. If a wreck occurs in the vicinity of Yarmouth, a considerable time must elapse before a boat can reach the wreck from St. John, and if an arrangement were made with this Yarmouth firm I believe it would result in the saving of lives and property. I hope that before long the minister will see his way to make such an arrangement as I have suggested.
What are the arrangements with the wrecking company on the lower St. Lawrence

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Quebec Salvage and Wrecking Company maintains the Lord Strathcona and such other craft as may be 
required to the satisfaction of the department, from the 1st of May to the 1st of November each year, on payment of a subsidy subject to certain conditions.

That applies to below
Quebec as well as to above Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Outside of the wreck of the Empress of Ireland, were the wrecks more numerous this year than last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Empress of Ireland
was the only wreck this year that was of any importance; the others were minor wrecks and little damage occurred.
Some of these wrecks were owing to defects in aids to navigation.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not think there was any such finding by the commissioner.

Was there any increase
in insurance rates up to the 1st of August last? .

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not think there way any appreciable increase up to the 1st of August.
Ocean and river service-Unforeseen expenses, $5,000.

I desire to call the
attention of the minister to a service rendered last year to the fishermen in the harbour of Ingonish. I do not know whether any claim has been put in for it with the department. In the early part of the year 1914, the fishing was very poor, but what they call the fall fishing was particularly good. It was made possible for the fishermen because a steam tug called the Nelson was fishing in the harbour and its owner broke the ice, making a track around the harbour which the gasoline and other boats could use and so get out to sea. In this way scores of boats were enabled to enjoy good fishing. The fishermen were talking of making a claim on the department for some slight recognition of the services rendered by the owner of this vessel. I should like to have thg Government bear the matter in mind if an application is made.'- The expense would be small.
Is there no application for life-saving stations?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That has been transferred to the Department of the Naval Service.

The minister will remember that at the last regular session I called his attention to the fact that there was not a single life-saving station on the whole

Gulf of St. Lawrence. I do not know if anything has been done since then. The minister will recognize the importance of having several such stations in the gulf.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have been considering the matter, and hope to meet the hon. gentleman's wish.

I desire, when the life-saving appropriation is under discussion to get some information. The boathouse of the life-saving service at Souris was moved, but I think that the present location is not as good as the former one. Also the building was somewhat injured in the removal. I wish to know how much it cost to remove this 'building, who recommended the removal, whether the new site has been purchased, and, if so, what it cost.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We will get the information for my hon. friend.
Progress reported.

Tuesday, February 23, 1915.
